For TileLang operator replacement, refer to this document . 1. Rotary Position Embedding Overview RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding) is a positional encoding operator used to compute rotary position embeddings in large models. Unlike conventional absolute positional encoding, RoPE integrates position information into the attention mechanism by rotating vectors, allowing it to better capture relative position relationships. This operator supports forward and backward propagation and applies to model training and inference scenarios. The following figure shows the overall Rotary Position Embedding computation process: Rotary Position Embedding Computation Flow Detailed Algorithm Process Analysis of typical input and output tensor dimensions: x: [M, hiddensize] or [B, S, N, D], the input tensor. sin: [scrows, ropedim], the rotary sine-angle vector. cos: [scrows, ropedim], the rotary cosine-angle vector. mask: [rowpervec, ropedim], the rotary index mask vector. output: The rotary position encoding output tensor, with the same shape as the input. Computation process: 1. Data Loading and Preprocessing Block loading: Load input data into the UB buffer in blocks of blockM. The default blockM is 64 for float16/bfloat16 or 32 for float32. Partial RoPE support: When ropedim is smaller than hiddensize, apply rotary position encoding only to the last ropedim dimensions of the input tensor and keep the preceding dimstart dimensions unchanged. 2. Data Type Conversion Precision improvement: For float16/bfloat16 inputs, use T.tile.cast to convert the data to float32 for computation, ensuring numerical precision and stability. 3. sin/cos Loading Position index computation: Compute the corresponding sin/cos index based on headnum and the row position using rowsincos = (rowx // headnum) % scrows. Rotation angle loading: Load the corresponding sin and cos values into the UB buffer based on the computed index. 4. Rotation Operation Element rearrangement: Use T.tile.gather with mask to rearrange elements during rotation. The mask vector encodes the index mapping required for rotation. Rotation modes: interleave mode: Swap and rotate adjacent element pairs: rotate([x0, x1, x2, x3]) = [-x1, x0, -x3, x2]. half mode: Swap and rotate the first and second halves: rotate([x0, x1, x2, x3]) = [-x2, -x3, x0, x1]. 5. RoPE Computation Forward propagation: Perform rotary position encoding using out = x cos + rotate(x) sin. Backward propagation: Compute the backward gradient using dx = cos dy + swap(sinmasked dy). 6. Result Write-Back Type conversion: Convert the computation result from float32 back to the original data type (float16/bfloat16). Result storage: Write the result back to Global Memory in blocks. For partial RoPE, update only the last ropedim dimensions. 2. moetokenpermute Overview The following figure shows the overall MoeTokenPermute computation process: MoeTokenPermute Computation Flow In large language models based on the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, the number of tokens received by different experts changes dynamically. Token distribution operations (Token Permute / Scatter) can become a computation bottleneck because of intensive discontinuous memory access. As the only user-facing interface for this operator, the MoeTokenPermute class deeply fuses histogram statistics, global prefix-sum computation, and data rearrangement by using low-level NPU features. The operator shields users from low-level memory alignment and inter-core synchronization details. Users only provide tokens and routing indexes to efficiently obtain a token tensor arranged contiguously by expert and corresponding Scatter offset records. Interface Parameters To better understand the algorithm process, the complete interface parameter definitions of the MoeTokenPermute class are as follows: 1. Initialization parameters (init): numtokens: int, the total number of tokens in the input sequence. topK: int, the number of experts assigned to each token. For example, set it to 2 for Top-2 routing. hiddensize: int, the hidden-state vector dimension of a token. numexperts: int, the total number of experts in the model. The default value is 64. numouttokens: int, the expected output token capacity. If it is 0, the default allocation size is numtokens topK. NUMCORES: int, the number of physical NPU cores used. The default value is 24. TILEH: int, the hidden-layer block size for intra-core data partitioning. The default value is None, which automatically uses the full hiddensize length. dtype: str, the computation type of token data. The default value is "float16". 2. Invocation parameters (call): tokens: Tensor[numtokens, hiddensize], the original input token hidden-state tensor. indices: Tensor[numtokens topK], the one-dimensional flattened expert index tensor output by the routing network. 3. Output values: permout: Tensor[outlen, hiddensize], the token tensor rearranged by expert assignment, where the initialization parameter numouttokens determines outlen. sio: Tensor[numtokens topK], the Scatter offset/write-position index corresponding to a token, excluding the invalid part of the low-level padding. Detailed Algorithm Process Based on the input and output parameters of the MoeTokenPermute class, the low-level operator runs as follows: 1. Tensor Initialization and Alignment Padding When call is invoked, first compute the logical total number of indexes E = numtokens topK. To meet the alignment requirements for even NPU multi-core partitioning, the operator computes an aligned length paddedE, which is a common multiple of NUMCORES and chunksize, and creates a padded index tensor indicespadded. It copies the user-provided indices into this tensor and pads the part beyond E with zeros. 2. Data Partitioning and Multi-Core Parallel Strategy Inter-core partitioning: Based on the NUMCORES specified during initialization, use the smaller of NUMCORES and numtokens as the actual number of cores and evenly divide the input token sequence across NPU cores. Each core processes a segment of token data with size tokenspercore and its corresponding index block (chunksize). Intra-core partitioning: For the hiddensize dimension, use the initialized TILEH to divide it into multiple sub-blocks (HTiles), and divide each sub-block in half (HALFH) across multiple vector compute units within one NPU core to implement finer-grained instruction-level parallelism. 3. Local Expert Histogram Statistics Each NPU core first asynchronously loads its assigned index data block from the global indicespadded. Use a pipelined loop to count the token frequency assigned to the numexperts experts in the data block (Histogram Count). After the statistics are complete, each core writes its local histogram result to the global Workspace and triggers a global synchronization Barrier to wait for all cores to finish statistics collection. 4. Global Offset Computation (Prefix Sum) Each core reads the complete histogram data from the global Workspace. Use two accumulations, the cumulative value of all cores accub and the preceding cumulative value of the current core cpreub, with the prefix-sum algorithm to compute the absolute base write offset (Scatter Offset) in the global output tensor permout for each token-expert pair on the current core. Store these offsets in the internal siochunkub array. 5. Pipelined Token Rearrangement (Pipelined Token Scatter) Construct a software pipeline buffer of size 2 (Double Buffering). Use flag synchronization between NPU asynchronous copy instructions (MTE2/MTE3) and vector computation instructions (V) to overlap memory reads with rearranged writes. In each loop, preload the next token data block from the input tokens tensor (MTE2). For the current token data block, query the write offset computed in step 4. If the offset is valid and does not exceed numouttokens, write the token data to the specified position in the output tensor permout (MTE3). 6. Result Extraction and Return After the pipeline is complete, the low-level operator outputs the padded rearranged token tensor and an index tensor recording global write positions. At the Python class interface layer, slice the valid Scatter indexes: sio = siopadded.squeeze(0)[:E]. Finally, return the rearranged contiguous token representation permout and offset record sio, completing the token arrangement process. 3. moetokenpermutegrad Overview The overall computation workflow of the MoeTokenPermuteGrad operator is shown in the following figure: MoeTokenPermuteGrad computation workflow During backpropagation in large language models based on the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, the token gradients calculated by each expert must be precisely propagated back to the original tokens according to the routing and dispatch rules used during forward propagation. Because one token may be routed to the Top-K experts during forward propagation, the gradient of the original token during backpropagation is the sum of the gradient vectors corresponding to these K experts (the Gather-Reduce operation). The MoeTokenPermuteGrad class is a fused operator for this operation. It uses the NPU's highly concurrent read/write capabilities and on-core accumulators to efficiently collect and merge gradients in reverse through the "batch index loading -> vector aggregation (Gather) -> high-precision accumulation (Reduce)" computation paradigm. To address numerical overflow or precision truncation that can easily occur in half-precision computation (such as float16), the operator specifically implements an accumulation mechanism with type upcasting (Cast to FP32) to ensure the numerical stability of gradient computation. Interface Parameters The complete interface parameter definitions of the MoeTokenPermuteGrad class are as follows: 1. Initialization parameters (init): numtokens: int, total number of tokens in the original input sequence. topK: int, number of experts to which each token is assigned during forward propagation. hiddensize: int, hidden-layer vector dimension of a token. numexperts: int, total number of experts in the model. The default value is 64 and is mainly used to maintain API symmetry in the backward operator. numouttokens: int, total token length output by forward propagation. If it is set to 0, it defaults to numtokens topK. NUMCORES: int, number of physical NPU cores to use. The default value is 24. TILEH: int, hidden-layer block size for on-core data partitioning. The default value is None (the optimal size is automatically derived based on hiddensize and the data type). dtype: str, data type of the input gradient. The default value is "float16". 2. Call parameters (call): permutedoutputgrad: Tensor[outlen, hiddensize], gradient corresponding to the forward-propagation output tensor, that is, the contiguous gradient tensor output by expert-layer backpropagation. sortedindices: Tensor[numtokens topK], offset/target-position indices generated by the forward Scatter operator (corresponding to the forward sio output). 3. Return value: inputgrad: Tensor[numtokens, hiddensize], token gradient tensor propagated back to the original input after Gather-Reduce aggregation and accumulation. -- Algorithm Workflow The gradient aggregation workflow of the MoeTokenPermuteGrad class is as follows: 1. Tensor initialization and alignment padding When call is invoked, first calculate the theoretical forward logical length E = numtokens topK. If the actual length of the passed permutedoutputgrad is less than E, the operator creates an all-zero padding tensor permgradpadded to pad the length and prevent out-of-bounds access during Gather. At the same time, pad and align the user-provided sortedindices to the paddedE length required for even NPU multi-core distribution. 2. Data partitioning and multi-core parallelization strategy Inter-core partitioning (Core-level): Calculate actualcores based on NUMCORES (use the smaller of NUMCORES and numtokens as the actual number of cores). Partition along the original token dimension. Each core restores the gradients of tokenspercore original tokens. Batch dimension (Batch-level): To prevent Unified Buffer (UB) overload, further partition the tokens assigned to each core into multiple batches (BATCHT) for batch-wise computation. Intra-core partitioning (Thread-level): Along the hiddensize dimension, the operator partitions data into multiple sub-blocks (nhtiles) and further divides each sub-block in half (HALFH = TILEH // 2) within a single compute core for parallel accumulation by two compute units. 3. Batched index loading Enter the serial batch-processing loop in units of BATCHT. Each NPU core asynchronously loads the expert routing indices corresponding to the current batch (with a size of BATCHT topK) from sortedidxgm into the Unified Buffer idxub. 4. Gradient aggregation and high-precision accumulation (Gather & Reduce) This is the core computation module of the backward operator. Based on the dtype specified during initialization, it routes execution to two different kernel functions (Cast and NoCast): High-precision accumulation mode (for float16 input): For a hiddensize block of the current token, first initialize an all-zero float32 accumulator (accbuf) in the buffer. Iterate topK times. Based on the loaded indices, use asynchronous copy (MTE2) to precisely fetch the corresponding Top-K gradient vector block from global memory permgradgm into rowbuf. Convert (Cast) the fetched float16 gradient vector to the high-precision float32 type (CASTLOW2HIGH) through a Vector Instruction. Accumulate the vector into accbuf at float32 precision to prevent small gradients from being lost or overflow caused by half-precision addition. After accumulation is complete, convert the result back to the float16 data format through CASTHIGH2LOW. Standard accumulation mode (for float32 input): If the input is already single-precision, omit the Cast overhead and directly use shared memory with loop unrolling for contiguous loading and addition. 5. Writing back the result After block-wise accumulation along the hiddensize dimension for a single token is complete, trigger a memory-to-global-memory write-back barrier (pipebarrier). Output the merged and restored gradient from the internal buffer and write it to the corresponding original-token position in global memory inputgradgm. The Python layer receives the final aggregated inputgrad tensor, which continues to participate in network backpropagation. 4. moetokenunpermute Overview The overall computation workflow of the MoeTokenUnpermute operator is shown in the following figure: MoeTokenUnPermute computation workflow In the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, after tokens are processed by different experts, the token features scattered across the output tensors of these experts must be gathered and combined according to their positions in the original sequence. If a Top-K routing strategy is used, the outputs obtained for the same token from multiple experts must also be multiplied by their corresponding Routing Probabilities and combined through a weighted sum (Reduce). The MoeTokenUnpermute class is the NPU operator interface that performs the preceding operation. This operator is developed based on the TileLang framework and is deeply optimized for the underlying hardware's Vector Unit and memory-copy path. During probability weighting, it also enforces a high-precision accumulation strategy with upcasting (Cast to FP32) to ensure numerical stability during model computation. Interface Parameters The complete interface parameter definitions of the MoeTokenUnpermute class are as follows: 1. Initialization parameters (init): numtokens: int, total number of tokens in the original input sequence. topK: int, number of experts assigned to each token (that is, the number of experts from which results for the same token must be fetched and aggregated). hiddensize: int, hidden-layer vector dimension of a token. hasprobs: bool, with a default value of True. Indicates whether weighted merging based on routing probabilities is required. If it is True, the operator performs Gather + Scale + Accumulate. If it is False, the operator performs only data gathering (Gather). paddedmode: bool, with a default value of False. Reserved parameter. Setting it to True is not currently supported and raises NotImplementedError. NUMCORES: int, number of physical NPU cores to use. The default value is 24. TILET: int, optional. Block size for partitioning along the on-core token dimension. The default value is None (the system dynamically calculates the optimal partition based on the total number of tokens). TILEH: int, optional. Block size for partitioning along the on-core hidden-layer dimension. The default value is None (the system automatically derives an aligned size). dtype: str, computation data type. The supported values are "float16", "bfloat16", "float32", and "float". The default value is "float16". 2. Call parameters (call): permutedtokens: Tensor[E, hiddensize] (where E = numtokens topK), collection of token tensors output after processing by the expert layers. sortedindices: Tensor[E], expert-index mapping recorded during the original permutation operation (that is, the mapping between token positions after permutation and their original positions). probs: Tensor[numtokens, topK], optional. Top-K routing probabilities corresponding to the tokens. This parameter is required when hasprobs=True. 3. Return value: out: Tensor. When hasprobs=True, returns the aggregated and weighted tensor with a shape of [numtokens, hiddensize]. When hasprobs=False, returns only the tensor obtained through Gather without summation-based dimension reduction. Its shape is [E, hiddensize]. Algorithm Workflow 1. Tensor initialization and dimension alignment (Padding) The underlying hardware often has minimum dimension requirements for parallel partitioning (for example, hiddensize must be at least 64 for float16). During initialization, the operator calculates compilehiddensize. When call is invoked, the padlastdim and padfirstdim functions dynamically pad the end of permutedtokens and the beginning of sortedindices, so that the total length and hidden-layer dimension are exact multiples (paddedE and paddedtokens) required for inter-core parallel distribution on the NPU. After computation, the Padding is removed by slicing the output. 2. Partitioning and scheduling strategy (Auto Tiling) Inter-core parallelism: Based on the state of hasprobs, the operator uses different parallel distribution strategies. autolaunchcores dynamically calculates the actual number of physical cores to activate (actualcores) and evenly distributes logical token blocks (nttiles or netiles) to the corresponding compute cores. Intra-core pipeline: Using the TILEH and TILET parameters automatically generated by TileLang, each compute core processes data in batches (BATCHT) and partitions the data flow into double buffers within the NPU core for processing by the vector unit. 3. Index parsing and data gathering (Index Gather) Each NPU compute core loads the corresponding routing probabilities probsub and inverse-sort indices idxub from global memory. Based on the loaded idxub, the compute core locates the row in permutedtokens where the token resides after expert computation and asynchronously fetches the corresponding feature row into the row buffer (rowbuf) in the Unified Buffer (UB) through data-copy instructions. 4. High-precision probability weighting and accumulation (Scale & Accumulate) If hasprobs=True: Type promotion (Cast-Up): To prevent severe precision truncation caused by repeated accumulation of half-precision floating-point values (FP16/BF16), the operator preallocates a high-precision buffer (accdtype, typically FP32) in the UB. It uses the CASTLOW2HIGH instruction to promote the precision of the feature data and probabilities probs. Multiply-add operation (AXPY): Expand the inner loop for the Top-K count. Because the Top-K value may not be an optimal multiple for instruction registers, the underlying implementation uses nquads (4-iteration/8-iteration loop unrolling) and remainder (remainder handling) to split computation into multiple suboperations. It uses the NPU's T.tile.axpy ($Y = aX + Y$) or T.tile.mul vector multiplication to multiply the current expert feature row by probability prob and accumulate it into the corresponding token accumulation register accbuf. Type demotion (Cast-Down): After the results from the Top-K experts for the same token are accumulated, use CASTHIGH2LOW to convert them back to the original data type (such as FP16). If hasprobs=False: Skip type conversion and accumulation, and directly write the expert features loaded into rowbuf back to the result buffer outgm row by row according to the partitioned dimensions. 5. Writing the result back to global memory Use the underlying pipebarrier to synchronize the scalar and vector instruction streams. After confirming that the current batch has been correctly computed in the registers, flush the data segments that have completed Unpermute (and Reduce) back to global memory. After all cores finish running, the interface slices off the initial Padding and returns a properly shaped output tensor. 5. moetokenunpermutegrad Overview The overall computation workflow of the MoeTokenUnpermuteGrad operator is shown in the following figure: MoeTokenUnPermuteGrad computation workflow During backpropagation in the Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, the gradients of the Token Unpermute (weighted aggregation) operation must be calculated. If Top-K routing and probability weighting (hasprobs=True) are used during forward propagation, the backward process must calculate gradients in two directions: 1. Gradient with respect to expert outputs (permgrad): According to the chain rule, it equals the gradient propagated from the upper layer multiplied by the corresponding routing probability. 2. Gradient with respect to routing probabilities (probsgrad): It equals the sum of the dot products between the gradient propagated from the upper layer and the corresponding expert output features (permutedtokens) along the hidden-layer dimension. The MoeTokenUnpermuteGrad class is the NPU operator interface that performs the preceding backward-gradient computation. This operator implements efficient data Scatter distribution and also optimizes the underlying multi-core parallelism and independent accumulation by the Dual-Vector Unit for the "dot product and reduction (Reduce Sum)" operation of probability gradients. This maximizes hardware throughput while ensuring high-precision FP32 accumulation. Interface Parameters The complete interface parameter definitions of the MoeTokenUnpermuteGrad class are as follows: 1. Initialization parameters (init): numtokens: int, total number of tokens in the original input sequence. topK: int, number of experts assigned to each token. hiddensize: int, hidden-layer vector dimension of a token. hasprobs: bool, with a default value of True. Indicates whether probability weighting was used during forward propagation. If it is True, the operator calculates and returns permgrad and probsgrad. If it is False, the operator only performs Scatter distribution of gradients and returns permgrad. NUMCORES: int, number of physical NPU cores to use. The default value is 24. TILET: int, optional. Block size for partitioning along the on-core token dimension. The default value is None (the system automatically calculates the optimal value). TILEH: int, optional. Block size for partitioning along the on-core hidden-layer dimension. The default value is None (the system automatically calculates the optimal aligned value). dtype: str, computation data type. The supported values are "float16", "bfloat16", "float32", and "float". The default value is "float16". 2. Call parameters (call): permutedtokens: Tensor[E, hiddensize] (where $E = num	okens 	imes topK$), token collection output by expert-layer computation during forward propagation. This parameter is required for calculating probability gradients when hasprobs=True. unpermutedtokensgrad: Tensor[numtokens, hiddensize], gradient corresponding to the output of the Unpermute operation that is propagated back from an upper network layer during backpropagation (that is, $ rac{\partial L}{\partial X{out}}$). sortedindices: Tensor[E], global indices that map routing relationships. probs: Tensor[numtokens, topK], optional. Top-K routing probabilities during forward propagation. This parameter is required when hasprobs=True. 3. Return value: When hasprobs=True, returns a tuple (permgrad, probsgrad): permgrad: Tensor[E, hiddensize], feature gradients propagated to the expert layers. probsgrad: Tensor[numtokens, topK], probability gradients propagated to the routing network (Router). When hasprobs=False, returns only: permgrad: Tensor[E, hiddensize]. -- Algorithm Workflow 1. Tensor initialization and dimension alignment (Padding) As with the forward operator, the underlying NPU hardware has alignment requirements for parallel block (Tile) sizes. When called on the Python side, the operator uses padfirstdim and padlastdim to dynamically pad the returned gradient unpermutedtokensgrad, expert features permutedtokens, indices, and probabilities at their first and last dimensions to paddedE and compilehiddensize. 2. Backward rearrangement and data distribution loading (Scatter Routing) Each NPU compute core loads the corresponding sortedidxgm and probsgm into the Unified Buffer (UB) based on its assigned token block. Based on the indices, the core locates the current row of unpermutedtokensgrad (the gradient propagated back from the upper network layer). 3. Highly concurrent gradient computation (Gradient Computation) If hasprobs=True: The operator uses a double-buffered pipeline to hide memory latency and divides computation into two paths: Calculate expert-feature gradients (permgrad): Extract the corresponding routing probability prob, promote it to a high-precision type (such as FP32) through CASTLOW2HIGH, and then perform vector multiplication $grad 32 	imes prob$. Demote the computation result (CASTHIGH2LOW) and write it back to global memory through the asynchronous MTE3 instruction. Calculate routing-probability gradients (probsgrad): Calculate the dot product of the gradient and features. The operator obtains the product for each dimension through vector multiply-add $grad 32 	imes perm 32$, then invokes the T.reducesum instruction to accumulate it along the hidden-layer dimension into the scalar register reducedst, and finally accumulates it into pgacc. If hasprobs=False: The operator enters a minimal mode (buildscatterkernelnoprobs). It does not calculate dot products or multiply by probabilities and only performs an index-based Scatter operation to copy segments of unpermutedtokensgrad to specified positions in permgrad. 4. Dual-vector-unit fusion (Dual-Vector Unit Optimization) In the NPU architecture, a single core usually contains two independent vector compute units (Vector Unit 0 and 1). To overcome the hardware bottleneck of dot-product Reduce operations, the operator adds a vid dimension when allocating probsgradgm at the underlying layer (changing its shape to [2, paddedtokens, topK]). The two vector units separately perform dot-product accumulation over HALFH (that is, half of the hidden-layer dimension) and retain their own Partial Sums. This design avoids frequent lock synchronization between the two execution units within a core. 5. Writing back results and dimension reduction on the Python side After the underlying kernel finishes execution, control returns to the Python-side interface. If probability calculation is enabled, the interface extracts the two probsgradraw results independently calculated by the NPU's dual vector units and performs probsgradraw[0] + probsgradraw[1] to add the two partial dot-product sums and complete the final Reduce Sum. Finally, slice all gradient tensors (permgrad and probsgrad) to remove the Padding introduced in step 1 and safely return them to the PyTorch computation graph in the original data type dtype. 6. rms norm Overview The overall computation workflow of the rms norm operator is shown in the following figure: rmsnorm computation workflow Root Mean Square Layer Normalization (RMS Norm) is an efficient normalization operator. It omits the mean-centering operation in LayerNorm and performs normalization using only the variance. Algorithm Workflow Analysis of typical input and output tensor dimensions for the operator: A: [M, N], input feature-matrix tensor. B: [M, N], normalized output feature-matrix tensor. blockM / blockN: Hyperparameters that specify row and column sizes for block-wise computation. dtype: Data type of the input and output. Computation workflow: 1. Precision alignment Memory allocation: Allocate the input buffer aub, computation buffer aubcast, and intermediate-variable storage in the Unified Buffer. Precision determination: Determine accdtype based on dtype and determine whether precision conversion is required. 2. Sum-of-squares accumulation Iterate over the column dimension by blockN, and use the mul and add operators to square feature values and accumulate them into sumsqacc: for by in T.serial(nnum): ​T.tile.mul(aubcast, aubcast, aubcast) T.tile.add(sumsqacc, sumsqacc, aubcast) 3. Reduction Perform row reduction (ReduceSum) on the sum-of-squares result to calculate the sum of squares of all column elements in each row. Store the reduction result in sumsqrow. 4. Calculating the reciprocal root mean square Mean calculation: Allocate the input buffer aub, computation buffer aubcast, and intermediate-variable storage in the Unified Buffer. Numerical stability processing: Add eps to prevent a zero value during subsequent square root and division operations. Reciprocal square root calculation: Execute the rsqrt instruction to obtain the scaling factor invrmsub for each row. 5. Applying normalization and writing back the result After pre-broadcasting, iterate over the column dimension again and read the original input. Vector multiplication: Perform element-wise multiplication of invrmstile and the input data to implement normalization: aubcast = aubcast invrmstile Precision restoration and result write-back: Convert the computation result back to the original dtype and write back the result. 7. swiglu Overview SwiGLU (Swish-Gated Linear Unit) is an activation operator commonly used in Transformers and large models. It enhances feature representation through a gating mechanism. The operator splits the input tensor into two parts along a specified dimension. One part passes through the Swish (SiLU) activation function, while the other serves as the gating vector. The two parts are multiplied element-wise to produce the output. The overall computation workflow of the swiglu operator is shown in the following figure: swiglu computation workflow Algorithm Workflow Analysis of typical input and output tensor dimensions for the operator: A: [M, N], input feature-matrix tensor. B: [M/mdiv, N/ndiv], output feature-matrix tensor. blockM / blockN: Hyperparameters that specify row and column sizes for block-wise computation. splitdim: Hyperparameter that specifies the partition dimension. By default, partitioning is performed by column. A value of 0 or -2 specifies row partitioning. dtype: Data type of the input and output. Computation workflow: 1. Block partitioning and parallel scheduling Partition the input tensor into multiple tiles by (blockM, blockN): blockid → (bx, by) Each tile corresponds to: Row start: rowstart = bx blockM Column start: colstart = by blockN Each core processes multiple tiles in a strided manner: blockid = cid + i NUMCORES Within each tile, further partition data along the row direction by VECNUM=2: rowspervec = blockM / 2 2. Data loading (Global → UB) For each tile: Load x1: x1 = A[rowstart, colstart] Load x2 (implement the split through an offset): x2 = A[rowstart + moffset, colstart + noffset] Column partitioning: noffset = N/2 Row partitioning: moffset = M/2 Data type conversion (optional) If the input is bf16/float16: x1ub = cast(x1 → float32) x2ub = cast(x2 → float32) Otherwise, directly use the original data. 3. Swish activation computation Swish(x1) =  rac{x1}{1 + e^{-x1}} In this stage, Swish is calculated element-wise in the UB. 1. Negate x1: temp = 0 - x1 (T.tile.sub) 2. Calculate the exponential: temp = exp(temp) (T.tile.exp) 3. Add 1 to construct the denominator: temp = temp + 1 (T.tile.add) 4. Calculate the reciprocal: temp = reciprocal(temp) (T.tile.reciprocal) 5. Multiply by the original x1: swish = x1 temp (T.tile.mul) The entire process is completed in the UB without additional memory access. 4. Gating computation (GLU) y=Swish(x1)⋅x2 Multiply the Swish output and x2 element-wise: result = swish x2 (T.tile.mul) 5. Writing back the result If lower precision is required: float32 → bf16 (T.tile.cast (CASTRINT)) Write back the output: B[rowstart, colstart] = result 8. swiglugrad Overview The SwiGLU Backward operator calculates gradients for the input tensor during forward propagation. Its core operation is differentiating the Swish activation function and combining it with the gating branch to calculate the gradients of the two components (x1 and x2). The overall computation workflow of the swiglugrad operator is shown in the following figure: swiglugrad computation workflow Algorithm Workflow Analysis of typical input and output tensor dimensions for the operator: A: [M, N], input feature-matrix tensor. dY: [M/mdiv, N/ndiv], upstream gradient. dA: [M, N], output gradient. blockM / blockN: Hyperparameters that specify row and column sizes for block-wise computation. splitdim: Hyperparameter that specifies the partition dimension. By default, partitioning is performed by column. A value of 0 or -2 specifies row partitioning. dtype: Data type of the input and output. Computation workflow: 1. Block partitioning and parallel scheduling Partition the input tensor into multiple tiles by (blockM, blockN): blockid → (bx, by) Each tile corresponds to: Row start: rowstart = bx blockM Column start: colstart = by blockN Each core processes multiple tiles in a strided manner: blockid = cid + i NUMCORES Within each tile, further partition data along the row direction by VECNUM=2: rowspervec = blockM / 2 2. Data loading (Global → UB) For each tile: Load x1: x1 = A[rowstart, colstart] Load x2 (implement the split through an offset): x2 = A[rowstart + moffset, colstart + noffset] Column partitioning: noffset = N/2 Row partitioning: moffset = M/2 Data type conversion (optional) If the input is bf16/float16: x1ub = cast(x1 → float32) x2ub = cast(x2 → float32) dyub = cast(dy → float32) Otherwise, directly use the original data. 3. Calculating the Swish derivative The Swish calculation is the same as in forward computation: Swish(x1) =  rac{x1}{1 + e^{-x1}} Where: σ(x1​)= rac{1}{1 + e^{-x1}} Swish derivative: Swish′(x1)=σ(x1)+x1⋅σ(x1)(1−σ(x1)) First process x1 element-wise: 1. Calculate the negative value (for the exponential calculation): temp = 0 - x1 2. Calculate the exponential: temp = exp(temp) 3. Add 1 to construct the denominator: temp = temp + 1 4. Calculate the reciprocal to obtain sigmoid: temp = reciprocal(temp). At this point, temp is sigmoid(x1). Then multiply it by the original x1 to obtain the Swish output: swish = x1 sigmoid This process corresponds to consecutive exp / add / reciprocal / mul Tile instructions. 4. Calculating dx2 Formula: dx2=dy⋅Swish(x1) First, multiply the swish result from the preceding step by the upstream gradient dy element-wise: dx2 = dy swish This part is an element-wise multiplication corresponding to T.tile.mul. 5. Calculating dx1 Formula: dx1=dy⋅x2⋅Swish′(x1) First, multiply the upstream gradient by gating branch x2: dx1 = dy x2 Then multiply by the Swish derivative: dx1 = dx1 swishgrad This operation is essentially two consecutive element-wise multiplications corresponding to two T.tile.mul instructions. 6. Writing back the result As in the forward operation, perform data type conversion through cast if necessary. Write dx1 back to the position corresponding to x1: dA[rowstart, colstart] = dx1 Write dx2 back to the position corresponding to x2 (with an offset): dA[rowstart + moffset, colstart + noffset] = dx2 Future Plan Usability Improvements Support a more complete set of NPU operators: Support all common NPU operators (Q4 2025) Generalization Enhancements Support dynamic shapes and full-network integration (Q4 2025) Add more configurable parameters to primitives Performance Optimization Optimize the performance of key operators: Further optimize the performance of the SparseFlashAttention and LightningIndexer operators so that typical-shape performance surpasses Triton (Q4 2025)

\sum{j=4(i+1)}^{4(i+2)-1}{e^{Zj^b+B{j-4i}}}} \\ &= \left[1\right]{1\times8} @ (softmax(\left[Z^a{\left[4(i-1)+1:4i,:\right]} ; Z^b{\left[4i+1:4(i+1),:\right]}\right] + B) \odot \left[C^a{\left[4(i-1)+1:4i,:\right]} ; C^b{\left[4i+1:4(i+1),:\right]}\right]) \end{aligned} $$ 其中 $B \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times d}$ 为 $C^a, C^b$ 对应的positional biases。 C4A 示意图 C128A层 相比C4A, C128A层的 Compressor 会以更大的压缩比率对KV序列去进行压缩，并且只依赖单一KV序列$C \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times d}$和压缩权重$Z \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times d}$，其中 $$ \begin{aligned} C&=X\cdot W^{KV}, \\ Z&=X\cdot W^{Gate} \end{aligned} $$ $W^{KV}, W^{Z}$ 是C128A对应KV和压缩权重的权重参数。 然后长度为$s$的KV序列$C$中的每 $128$ 个$KV$会被压缩成 $1$ 个 $C^{\text{Comp}} \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{s}{128} \times d}$，其第 $i$ 行 $$ \begin{aligned} C{i}^{\text{Comp}} &= \frac{\sum{j=128i}^{128(i+1)-1}{e^{Zj+B{j-128i}}} \odot Cj}{\sum{j=128i}^{128(i+1)-1}{e^{Zj+B{j-128i}}}} \\ &= \left[1\right]{1\times128} @ (softmax(Z{\left[128(i-1)+1:128i,:\right]} + B) \odot C{\left[128(i-1)+1:128i,:\right]}) \end{aligned} $$ $i = 1, \cdots, \frac{s}{128},$ 其中 $B \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times d}$ 为 $C$ 对应的positional biases. C128A 示意图 具体计算流程 Compressor 会先把 $r (r=4 \text{ or } 128)$ 个$KV$压缩成 $1$ 个，再对压缩后的 $KV$ 做 RMSNorm 与 Partial Rope 的后处理。各阶段具体计算如下： 压缩阶段： 1. 计算矩阵乘法： C4A: $\left[C^a, Z^a\right] = X @ \left[W^{aKV}, W^{aGate}\right], \left[C^b, Z^b\right] = X @ \left[W^{bKV}, W^{bGate}\right];$ C128A: $\left[C, Z\right] = X @ \left[W^{KV}, W^{Gate}\right]$ 2. 计算分组加法： C4A: $Zi^\prime = \left[Z{\left[4(i-1)+1:4i,:\right]}^a; Z{\left[4i+1:4(i+1),:\right]}^b\right]+B,i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{4};$ C128A: $Zi^\prime = Z{\left[128(i-1)+1:128i,:\right]} + B,i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{128};$ 3. 计算分组Softmax： C4A: $Si^\prime = softmax(Zi^\prime),i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{4};$ C128A: $Si^\prime = softmax(Zi^\prime),i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{128};$ 4. 计算Hadamard乘积: C4A: $(SH)i = Si^\prime \odot \left[C^a{\left[4(i-1)+1:4i,:\right]} ; C^b{\left[4i+1:4(i+1),:\right]}\right],i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{4};$ C128A: $SH = S^\prime \odot C;$ 5. 沿着压缩轴分组求和： C4A: $C{i}^{\text{Comp}} = \left[1\right]{1\times8} @ (SH)i, i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{4};$ C128A: $C{i}^{\text{Comp}} = \left[1\right]{1\times128} @ (SH)i, i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{128};$ 后处理阶段： 1. 计算RMSNorm; 2. 计算Partial RoPE。 Query 对应的 $Q{index}\in\R^{n \times Sq \times d}$，给定上下文 Index Key $K{index}\in\R^{S{k}\times d},W\in\R^{n \times Sq\times 1}$，其中 $n$ 为头的个数，$d$ 为每一个头的维度，$S{q}$ 是请求的个数，$S{k}$ 三个维度上相乘, $\odot$ 代表逐元素相乘)： 1. 对量化后的矩阵计算矩阵乘法：$S = Q{index}@{d} K{index}^T$； 2. 计算激活函数：$S'=\text{ReLU}(S)$； 3. W 吸收反量化系数 $Scaleq$：$W' = Scaleq \odot W$; 4. 计算广播乘法：$SW=(W' @{1}[1]{1\times S{k}})\odot S'$； 5. 关于头进行ReduceSum操作：$Score=[1]{1\times n}@{n} SW$； 6. 广播乘反量化系数：$Score = (Scalek @{1}[1]{1\times S{q}})^T \odot Score$ 7. 对 $Score$ 进行 $\text{Top-}k$ 计算，即获取数值排序前 $k$ 个的结果，并返回其对应的 Index。 在 Prefill 或开启 MTP 的 Decode 场景，多个 token 对应的 $Q{index}$ 会被合并统一计算，本文后续部分不对单/多个 token 对应的 $Q{index}$ 加以区分。 scheduler 算子 对于 Attention 及 LI 这类“值依赖算子”而言，仅依靠输入的 shape 信息无法实现好的分核策略，还需要在运行时获取实际的上下文长度。传统 Scheduler 实现方式需要回到 HOST 执行，会导致整体执行流水被打断；而直接在算子 kernel 内计算分核策略会导致这一部分的计算耗时无法被掩盖，引入极大的头开销。昇腾芯片内置若干个 ARM 计算核（AICPU），把这一部分 Scheduler 计算放到 AICPU 上执行既可以保证算子入图又可以使得这一部分耗时被掩盖。 本次同步发布了SparseAttnSharedKV及LightningIndexer对应的AICPU Scheduler 算子: SAS AICPU Scheduler , LI AICPU Scheduler 。 现可以将整个 Scheduler 过程分为两个部分： 具体的分核策略：每个核要执行的实际计算部分，提高计算负载的均衡性以实现高算力利用率。 第一个部分的 Scheduler 计算由 Host 执行，而本次算子将第二个值依赖部分的 Scheduler 单独定义为一个 AICPU 算子，其输出蕴含分核信息的 metadata 供实际的 NPU 算子使用： python run in aicpu metadata = torchnpu.npusparseattnsharedkvmetadata(......) run in aicore npuresult, softmaxlse = torch.ops.custom.npusparseattnsharedkv(...,metadata=metadata,...) 这样的方式有很多优势： 更为灵活，不需要框架侧额外识别这类特殊的“值依赖”算子，也减轻了算子侧额外适配框架的工作量； 用户通过脚本直接调用 AICPU 算子即可，对于 aclgraph 等图模式更为友好； 对于单次推理而言，每种计算模式对应的 AICPU Scheduler 算子只需要执行一次，可以复用。 对于同样有实时 Scheduler 需求的算子，也可以自定义开发 AICPU Scheduler NPU DeepSeek-V4 Ascend C Fused Operator Optimization For the DeepSeek-V4 architecture, this release introduces two new fused operators, SparseAttnSharedKV (SAS) and Compressor, and enhances the capabilities of LightningIndexer (LI). The SparseAttnSharedKV operator is designed for the Attention module in the new DeepSeek architecture. It covers multiple FlashAttention application scenarios with SharedKV, including Sliding Window Attention, Compressed Attention, Sparse Attention, and their combinations. The computation workflow and core functions of the LightningIndexer operator remain unchanged. For $KV$ compression scenarios, it adapts the corresponding mask calculation method and uses the histogram API on 950PR/DT to accelerate Top-$k$ computation. The Compressor operator targets the complex compression algorithm in the new architecture and implements a series of originally separate operations as an efficient fused operator. All three operators support both the Atlas-A3 and 950PR/DT platforms and adapt to FP8 quantization mode on 950PR/DT to further improve CANN operator support for different data types. Highlights The fused operators are open-sourced for both Atlas-A3 and 950PR/DT, strengthening Ascend chip support for the low-precision FP8 floating-point type. Fuse the complex Compressor computation workflow while supporting different compression methods. Enhance the LightningIndexer operator and use new 950PR/DT instructions to improve operator performance. Use a unified interface design so that the SparseAttnSharedKV operator covers multiple Attention computation scenarios. Separate the value-dependent Scheduler computation into an AICPU Scheduler operator for more flexible use and adaptation to different graph modes. Use a staged core-partitioning strategy to fully use hardware computing resources. Attention modules in different layers use different computation modes and are divided into three categories based on each layer's compress ratio: C1A: The first two layers are C1A layers and only involve Sliding Window Attention computation on the original $KV$. Each token is computed only with the original $KV$ cache corresponding to the adjacent 128 tokens. C1A-Attention C4A: Odd-numbered layers except the first layer are C4A layers. In addition to Sliding Window Attention computation with a window size of 128 on the original $KV$ (oriKV), Attention in C4A layers also involves sparse computation with compressed $KV$ (cmpKV). cmpKV is compressed based on the semantics of every four tokens and their preceding four tokens. C4A-Attention C128A: Even-numbered layers except the second layer are C128A layers. In addition to Sliding Window Attention computation with a window size of 128 on the original $KV$ (oriKV), Attention in C128A layers also involves dense computation with compressed $KV$ (cmpKV). cmpKV is compressed based on the semantics of every 128 tokens. C128A-Attention In C4A and C128A layers, the input hidden state generates oriKV and cmpKV through a series of computations. The cmpKV computation workflow is complex and differs between the C4A and C128A scenarios. We designed this part of the computation as a Compressor fused operator on Atlas-A3 and 950PR/DT, supporting the computation workflows in different scenarios and achieving good performance. C4A layers further sparsify cmpKV. Continuing the DeepSeek-V3.2 design, this sparsification is based on LightningIndexer. The LightningIndexer fused operator released here adapts the staircase-shaped mask calculation logic corresponding to the compress ratio based on the original Atlas-A3 operator and adapts a fully FP8-quantized version on 950PR/DT. Because Attention computation differs across layers, multiple scenarios are involved. For the core Attention computation in DeepSeek-V4, we designed a new unquantized SparseAttnSharedKV operator on Atlas-A3 and a pseudo-quantized SparseAttnSharedKV operator on 950PR/DT, both supporting Attention Sink. A single interface covers different functional requirements. Compressor DeepSeek-V4 uses a new attention architecture: Compress-4-Attention (C4A) and Compress-128-Attention (C128A). Specifically, every 4 or 128 tokens in the $KV$ cache are compressed into one, and each token then performs Attention computation with these compressed $KV$ caches. For long sequences, C4A and C128A effectively reduce computation overhead. Formula C4A Layer The Compressor in a C4A layer contains the following series of computation operations. Given input $X\in \mathbb{R}^{s\times h}$, where $s$ is the sequence length and $h$ is the hidden size, first calculate its two corresponding $KV$ inputs $C^a, C^b \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times d}$ and compression weights $Z^a, Z^b \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times d}$, where $d$ is the head dimension. The formulas are as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} C^a&=X\cdot W^{aKV}, C^b=X\cdot W^{bKV}, \\ Z^a&=X\cdot W^{aGate}, Z^b=X\cdot W^{bGate}, \end{aligned} $$ Here, $W^{aKV}, W^{bKV}, W^{aGate}, W^{bGate} \in \mathbb{R}^{h \times d}$ are the KV and compression-weight parameters corresponding to C4A. Every four KV entries in the KV sequences $C^a, C^b$ of length $s$ are compressed into one $C^{\text{Comp}} \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{s}{4} \times d}$. The formula for its $i$-th row $C{i}^{\text{Comp}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1 \times d}$ is as follows: $$ \begin{aligned} C{i}^{\text{Comp}} &= \frac{\sum{j=4i}^{4(i+1)-1}{e^{Zj^a+B{j-4i}}} \odot C^aj + \sum{j=4(i+1)}^{4(i+2)-1}{e^{Zj^b+B{j-4i}}} \odot C^bj}{\sum{j=4i}^{4(i+1)-1}{e^{Zj^a+B{j-4i}}} + \sum{j=4(i+1)}^{4(i+2)-1}{e^{Zj^b+B{j-4i}}}} \\ &= \left[1\right]{1\times8} @ (softmax(\left[Z^a{\left[4(i-1)+1:4i,:\right]} ; Z^b{\left[4i+1:4(i+1),:\right]}\right] + B) \odot \left[C^a{\left[4(i-1)+1:4i,:\right]} ; C^b{\left[4i+1:4(i+1),:\right]}\right]) \end{aligned} $$ Here, $B \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times d}$ is the positional biases corresponding to $C^a, C^b$. C4A Diagram C128A Layer Compared with C4A, the Compressor in a C128A layer compresses the KV sequence at a higher compression ratio and depends only on a single KV sequence $C \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times d}$ and compression weight $Z \in \mathbb{R}^{s \times d}$, where: $$ \begin{aligned} C&=X\cdot W^{KV}, \\ Z&=X\cdot W^{Gate} \end{aligned} $$ $W^{KV}, W^{Z}$ are the KV and compression-weight parameters corresponding to C128A. Every 128 $KV$ entries in the KV sequence $C$ of length $s$ are then compressed into one $C^{\text{Comp}} \in \mathbb{R}^{\frac{s}{128} \times d}$. Its $i$-th row is: $$ \begin{aligned} C{i}^{\text{Comp}} &= \frac{\sum{j=128i}^{128(i+1)-1}{e^{Zj+B{j-128i}}} \odot Cj}{\sum{j=128i}^{128(i+1)-1}{e^{Zj+B{j-128i}}}} \\ &= \left[1\right]{1\times128} @ (softmax(Z{\left[128(i-1)+1:128i,:\right]} + B) \odot C{\left[128(i-1)+1:128i,:\right]}) \end{aligned} $$ $i = 1, \cdots, \frac{s}{128},$ where $B \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times d}$ is the positional biases corresponding to $C$. C128A Diagram Detailed Computation Workflow Compressor first compresses $r (r=4 \text{ or } 128)$ $KV$ entries into one and then postprocesses the compressed $KV$ through RMSNorm and Partial RoPE. Each stage is calculated as follows: Compression stage: 1. Calculate matrix multiplication: C4A: $\left[C^a, Z^a\right] = X @ \left[W^{aKV}, W^{aGate}\right], \left[C^b, Z^b\right] = X @ \left[W^{bKV}, W^{bGate}\right];$ C128A: $\left[C, Z\right] = X @ \left[W^{KV}, W^{Gate}\right]$ 2. Calculate grouped addition: C4A: $Zi^\prime = \left[Z{\left[4(i-1)+1:4i,:\right]}^a; Z{\left[4i+1:4(i+1),:\right]}^b\right]+B,i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{4};$ C128A: $Zi^\prime = Z{\left[128(i-1)+1:128i,:\right]} + B,i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{128};$ 3. Calculate grouped Softmax: C4A: $Si^\prime = softmax(Zi^\prime),i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{4};$ C128A: $Si^\prime = softmax(Zi^\prime),i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{128};$ 4. Calculate the Hadamard product: C4A: $(SH)i = Si^\prime \odot \left[C^a{\left[4(i-1)+1:4i,:\right]} ; C^b{\left[4i+1:4(i+1),:\right]}\right],i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{4};$ C128A: $SH = S^\prime \odot C;$ 5. Sum by group along the compression axis: C4A: $C{i}^{\text{Comp}} = \left[1\right]{1\times8} @ (SH)i, i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{4};$ C128A: $C{i}^{\text{Comp}} = \left[1\right]{1\times128} @ (SH)i, i=1,2,\cdots, \frac{s}{128};$ Postprocessing stage: 1. Calculate RMSNorm. 2. Calculate Partial RoPE. Fusion Benefits Compressor Computation Workflow As shown in the preceding computation workflow, Compressor contains many non-computational vector operations, such as split and slice. Implementing them as small operators would introduce large amounts of unnecessary repeated data movement in and out, resulting in extremely poor performance. A fused-operator implementation can perform these operations inline during data movement, substantially reducing the latency of the Compressor component. In the figure, coff is 1 in a C128A layer and 2 in a C4A layer. coff=2 means that the semantics of two adjacent groups of tokens are required for compression. Therefore, the Compressor in a C4A layer introduces a complex data-rearrangement operation: C4A Compressor Data Rearrangement As shown in the preceding figure, the Compressor in a C4A layer introduces a complex data-rearrangement operation. After each token is mapped to two vectors of size $d$ (the red and yellow blocks in the figure), the yellow-block vectors corresponding to every four tokens and the red-block vectors corresponding to the preceding four tokens are rearranged into contiguous storage. Implementing this operation separately with small operators would also introduce many non-computational vector operations. In this fused operator, this data rearrangement is implemented efficiently. For details, see Offset Write . Tiling Design Atlas-A3 Operator Tiling on Atlas-A3 is as follows: For C128A: L1 space is divided into the following parts: $X$ matrix: $2 \times 256 \times 256 \times 2 \text{ Bytes}=256 \text{ KB}$. The basic L1-level block is $(256, 256)$. $W^{KV}, W^{Gate}$ matrices: $2 \times 256 \times 64 \times 2 \text{ Bytes}=64 \text{ KB}$. The basic L1-level block is $(256, 128)$. Each iteration moves in two $(256, 64)$ matrix blocks for each of $W^{KV}$ and $W^{Gate}$. L0A and L0B enable double buffering and are divided into $2\times32\text{ KB}$ and $2\times32\text{ KB}$, respectively. The matrix block moved into each of L0A and L0B at a time has a size of $(128,128)$. L0C enables double buffering and is divided into $2\times64\text{ KB}$ to store the multiplication results of one $X$ block and the $W^{KV}, W^{Gate}$ matrices, which are accumulated in L0C. For C4A: L1 space is divided into the following parts: $X$ matrix: $128 \times 256 \times 2 \text{ Bytes}=64 \text{ KB}$. The basic L1-level block is $(128, 256)$. $W^{KV}, W^{Gate}$ matrices: $4 \times 256 \times 64 \times 2 \text{ Bytes}=128 \text{ KB}$. The basic L1-level block is $(256, 128)$. Each iteration moves in one $(256, 64)$ matrix block for each of $W^{aKV}$, $W^{bKV}$, $W^{aGate}$, and $W^{bGate}$. L0A and L0B enable double buffering and are divided into $2\times32\text{ KB}$ and $2\times32\text{ KB}$, respectively. The matrix block moved into each of L0A and L0B at a time has a size of $(128,128)$. L0C enables double buffering and is divided into $2\times64\text{ KB}$ to store the multiplication results of two $X$ blocks and one KV+Gate matrix, which are accumulated in L0C. On-Core Compressor Tiling on Atlas-A3 After matrix multiplication is completed on this basic block and accumulated along the reduce axis, the data is evenly distributed to two Vector cores for subsequent Vector operations. Decode During Decode, to resolve the inability to partition cores along the $s$ axis, further partition the $d$ axis from $64$ to $32$ to increase the number of started cores and bandwidth utilization. Basic-Block Cost Model Selecting the basic block is critical to operator design. An appropriate Tiling strategy must be determined through theoretical calculations based on hardware parameters: To overlap the time required to move the left or right matrix during one basic-block iteration with the corresponding computation time, the movement time must not exceed the computation time, that is: $$ \frac{(baseM + baseN) \times baseK \times 2 \text{ Bytes}}{\text{Bandwidth}} \leq \frac{baseM \times baseN \times baseK}{4096} $$ Cancel $baseK$ from both sides. For Atlas-A3, select $(baseM, baseN, baseK)=(256, 128, 512)$ in C128A and $(baseM, baseN, baseK)=(128, 256, 512)$ in C4A. The selection of $baseK$ primarily considers Ascend-friendly Cacheline alignment to improve movement efficiency. For 950PR/DT, considering L0A and L0B capacity constraints, $baseM=baseN=baseK=256$ can satisfy the condition. Offset Write When calculating C4A, note that the indices used by $Z^b, C^b$ to calculate $C{i}^{\text{Comp}}$ overlap the indices used by $Z^a, C^a$ to calculate $C{i+1}^{\text{Comp}}$. Offset write is used here to implement this processing. As shown in the following figure, after the preceding matrix multiplication is complete, an additional address offset is specified when the red computation results are written to the destination address. This aligns the red and yellow computation results. The data required from statecache can then be read into the UB for subsequent vector computation directly. Offset Write LightningIndexer Formula LightningIndexer obtains the Top-$k$ positions corresponding to each token through a series of operations. Ignoring the batch axis, for Query's $Q{index}\in\R^{n \times Sq \times d}$, given context Index Key $K{index}\in\R^{S{k}\times d},W\in\R^{n \times Sq\times 1}$, where $n$ is the number of heads, $d$ is the dimension of each head, $S{q}$ is the number of requests, and $S{k}$ is the context length, the formula for LightningIndexer is as follows: $$ \text{Top-}k\left\{[1]{1\times n}@n\left[(W@{1}[1]{1\times S{k}})\odot\text{ReLU}\left(Q{index}@{d}K{index}^T\right)\right]\right\} $$ Here, $Q{index}$ and $K{index}$ are assumed to be quantized FP8 (E4M3) matrices. During quantization, a dequantization coefficient is obtained for each head and each token and is expressed in matrix form as $Scaleq \in\R^{n \times Sq\times 1}$ and $Scalek \in \R^{Sk \times 1}$. LightningIndexer can be divided into the following computation workflow (where $@{d}$, $@{1}$, and $@{n}$ represent multiplication along the $d$, $1$, and $n$ dimensions, respectively, and $\odot$ represents element-wise multiplication): 1. Calculate matrix multiplication on the quantized matrices: $S = Q{index}@{d} K{index}^T$. 2. Calculate the activation function: $S'=\text{ReLU}(S)$. 3. W absorbs the dequantization coefficient $Scaleq$: $W' = Scaleq \odot W$. 4. Calculate broadcast multiplication: $SW=(W' @{1}[1]{1\times S{k}})\odot S'$. 5. Perform ReduceSum over the heads: $Score=[1]{1\times n}@{n} SW$. 6. Broadcast and multiply by the dequantization coefficient: $Score = (Scalek @{1}[1]{1\times S{q}})^T \odot Score$. 7. Perform $\text{Top-}k$ computation on $Score$, obtain the first $k$ results in value order, and return their corresponding Indices. In Prefill or Decode scenarios with MTP enabled, the $Q{index}$ values corresponding to multiple tokens are merged for unified computation. The following sections do not distinguish between $Q{index}$ corresponding to one or multiple tokens. In actual development, Ascend hardware features must be fully used to achieve better performance. The following sections describe the current solution and implementation in detail. Lightning Indexer Computation Workflow Tiling Design Atlas-A3 The Tiling of LightningIndexer on Atlas-A3 follows the previous design. For details, see Atlas-A3 LightningIndexer . Top-k Solution on 950PR/DT The core function of the LightningIndexer fused operator is to efficiently select the $k$ highest-scoring indices, such as 512, for each token from a sequence containing hundreds of thousands of entries (the sequence length is denoted by $S{k}$). For the operator, Top-$k$ computation must also be exact and cannot use an approximate algorithm. An Ascend-friendly solution is to use the Histograms instruction on 950PR/DT. This instruction performs histogram statistics on a group of uint8 numbers. In one cycle, it can place 64 numbers into buckets 0-127 or 128-255. Based on this approach and using one Query as an example, the core algorithm for selecting Top-$k$ from $S{k}$ float-type Scores using the Histograms instruction is summarized as follows: Order-Preserving Transformation Assume that $x$ is the binary representation of floating-point number $f$, and $\text{convert}(f)$ is the transformed uint32 value. The following order-preserving transformation algorithm can be used: c uint32t mask = (x&0x80000000)?0xffffffff:0x80000000; return (f==f)?(x^mask):0x0; This is equivalent to the following piecewise function: $$ \text{convert}(f) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if}\ f\ \text{is nan}\\ 2^{32}-1-x (\equiv \sim x) & \text{if}\ x\ \geq 2^{31} (\text{i.e.}\ f uint32 Example; uint16 Requires Only Two-Level Histograms As shown in the figure, the multi-level histogram workflow for selecting the Top-$k$ value is as follows: 1. For all uint32 elements, extract the first 8 bits from high to low and use the hist instruction to create a histogram. The returned result is an array Array1 of length 256, where the $i$-th value represents the sum of the numbers in buckets 0 through $i$. 2. Compare the values in Array1 with the threshold $Sk-k+1$. Positions greater than or equal to $Sk-k+1$ are true. The first true bucket in ascending order is the bucket containing the Top-$k$ element (the blue part in the figure), denoted by $a1$. Elements whose first 8 bits are less than $a1$ can now be masked out (the gray part in the figure). These elements are discarded. Let the number discarded in this step be $C1$ ($C1 The basic block size calculated in one iteration is (256,512), which completes computation over length 256 along the $Q$ sequence direction and length 512 along the $KV$ sequence direction. In actual scenarios, such as sparse computation in C4A layers, different $Q$ values cannot be merged along an axis and can only be computed together within one Group. Therefore, the actual basic block size calculated in one iteration may be (64,512), but this does not affect the overall Cache partitioning. The on-core operator Tiling design is as follows: L1 space is divided into the following parts: $Q/P$ matrices use time-division multiplexing ($P$ is the result of softmax computation): 4×128×256×2 Bytes=256 KB. During a $C1$ or $C2$ stage, the left matrix is moved into L1 in four batches and remains resident in L1 for one iteration. The movement size of the $Q$ matrix each time is (128,256), and that of the $P$ matrix is (128,256). $K/V$ matrices use cyclic 3-Buffer reuse: 3×128×256×2 Bytes=192 KB. The movement size of the $K$ matrix each time is (128,256), and that of the $V$ matrix is (256,128). L0A, L0B, and L0C enable Double Buffering and are divided into $2\times32\text{ KB}$ KB, $2\times32\text{ KB}$, and $2\times64\text{ KB}$, respectively. In the $C1$ / $C2$ stage, the matrix blocks moved into L0A and L0B at a time have sizes of (128,128) and (128,128), respectively. Multi-Scenario Coverage The SparseAttnSharedKV operator implements Attention computation for different scenarios through multiple input-parameter combinations. The key input parameters are: orikv: Original $KV$ cache corresponding to SWA. oriwinleft, oriwinright: Range along the sequence axis of the key-value entries participating in sliding window attention. Assume that $t$ is the sequence id of the query. The sequence id range of the participating key/value entries is $t - \text{win\left}, t - \text{win\left} + 1, ..., t, ..., t + \text{win\right}$. cmpkv: Compressed $KV$ cache of C4A and C128A layers. cmpratio: Compression ratio of $KV$ in cmpkv. The preceding input parameters can be combined as follows to perform Attention computation for different scenarios in DeepSeek-V4: AICPU Scheduler The Scheduler's core function is to statically simulate and control the execution flow. By preallocating global-memory space, locking execution branches, and optimizing the core-partitioning strategy, this mechanism effectively eliminates runtime overhead, keeps the instruction pipeline saturated, and substantially improves hardware throughput. AICPU Scheduler Operator For value-dependent operators such as Attention and LI, input shape information alone cannot produce a good core-partitioning strategy. The actual context length must also be obtained at runtime. A conventional Scheduler implementation must return to the HOST for execution, interrupting the overall execution pipeline. Calculating the core-partitioning strategy directly in the operator kernel prevents this computation latency from being overlapped and introduces substantial initial overhead. Ascend chips contain several ARM compute cores (AICPU). Running this Scheduler computation on AICPU ensures that the operator can be included in a graph and that this latency can be overlapped. This release also provides AICPU Scheduler operators corresponding to SparseAttnSharedKV and LightningIndexer: SAS AICPU Scheduler and LI AICPU Scheduler . The entire Scheduler process can now be divided into two parts: Calculations that require only the input shape: Maximum global-memory usage, max workspace: Used to allocate sufficient device space for the operator in advance. Specific execution path, tiling key: Determines the actual compiled operator template. Number of enabled cores, block dim: Determines the core-start configuration. tiling data: Extracts actual shape information for constant folding to reduce scalar computation at operator runtime. Calculations that require the actual context length: Specific core-partitioning strategy: Specifies the actual computation part performed by each core and improves computation-load balance to achieve high compute utilization. The first part of Scheduler computation is performed by the Host. This operator separately defines the second, value-dependent part of the Scheduler as an AICPU operator. Its output metadata contains core-partitioning information for use by the actual NPU operator: python run in aicpu metadata = torchnpu.npusparseattnsharedkvmetadata(......) run in aicore npuresult, softmaxlse = torch.ops.custom.npusparseattnsharedkv(...,metadata=metadata,...) This method provides many advantages: It is more flexible. The framework does not need to additionally identify these special value-dependent operators, and the operator requires less work to adapt to the framework. Users can directly invoke the AICPU operator through a script, making it more friendly to graph modes such as aclgraph. For a single inference operation, the AICPU Scheduler operator corresponding to each computation mode only needs to run once and can be reused. Operators that also require real-time scheduling can implement custom AICPU Scheduler operators to improve full-network performance. For the development method and more information, see AICPU Operator Development (Chinese).

NPU DeepSeek-V4 AutoFuse算子自动融合优化 随着AI模型结构日益复杂化，特别是MoE(混合专家)及多模态架构中，动态、细粒度的小算子组合已成为主流设计模式。DeepSeek本次发布的最新模型中，诸如hcPre、hcPost均是灵活小算子结构，未来在多模态场景类似结构也会成为常态。这类算子结构灵活多变，组合方式多样，若依赖传统手写融合算子方式进行优化，其开发效率已难以跟上模型快速迭代的需求。因此，实现对算子的自动化融合能力具有显著的技术必要性与紧迫性。 PyTorch框架在图模式下的Inductor组件为此提供了基础的算子融合与编译能力，其设计兼容现有PyTorch生态，具备良好的软件继承性。然而，由于NPU与GPU在内存架构、计算单元及并行机制等方面存在本质差异，直接沿用面向GPU的优化策略难以充分发挥NPU的硬件潜力。 为在继承Inductor整体流程与接口的基础上实现针对NPU的高效融合，需具备面向NPU的即时编译（JIT）算子生成能力。为此，CANN框架继承的AutoFuse组件针对NPU架构特征进行了深度优化，实现了从计算图到高效NPU算子代码的自动化映射与生成。该组件不仅保持与Inductor技术的协同与兼容，更进一步通过架构感知的融合策略、内存访问优化与指令调度等手段，显著提升了算子融合在NPU上的执行效率，从而支撑复杂模型在NPU平台上的高性能部署。 在本篇技术报告中，我们将对NPU的vector算子自动融合技术以及与inductor的对接工作进行阐述，同时简单介绍模型收益与使能方式。 Highlights 使用简单：PyTorch前端增加一行代码即可使能 性能提升：依赖NPU亲和的算子生成技术，提升模型开箱性能 亲和NPU，模板规约的schedule技术 基于硬件建模，动态求解的算子tiling技术 基于AscendLoopIR表达的，AscendC算子kernel代码生成技术 泛化与完备度：当前已支持152个LoopIR中的46个，未来将逐步补齐，与LoopIR完整对等 Outline NPU DeepSeek-V4 AutoFuse算子自动融合优化 Highlights Outline inductor与AutoFuse对接 AutoFuse JIT的算子生成能力 亲和NPU，模板规约的schedule技术 基于硬件建模，动态求解的算子tiling技术 基于AscendLoopIR表达的，AscendC算子kernel代码生成技术 AscendLoopIR简介 inductor与AutoFuse对接 我们扩展了inductor在NPU上的Codegen后端，通过将InductorLoopIR转换为AscendLoopIR，调用AutoFuse模块进行Schedule模板选择、UB复用与Tiling调优，生成高效的AscendC Kernel实现。 Inductor对接Autofuse的参考实现： inductornpuext 脚本使能方式 1. 在脚本开头导入 inductornpuext 以注册基于 Autofuse 的 inductor 编译后端扩展。 python import inductornpuext 2. 通过在函数上添加 @torch.compile 装饰以对函数进行编译，建议基于以下规则选择 inductor 编译范围： 编译范围内图结构稳定，不包含执行时分支选择、.item()内存同步等行为，避免过多的断图（Graph Break）。 避免编译范围过大，过大的编译范围由于 dynamo guard 叠加，更容易触发重新编译（re-compile）。 选择包含较多 Pintwise/Reduce 计算的范围进行编译，inductor 对该类计算的融合效果较好，能以较小的编译代价获取性能收益。 典型片段收益 在 DeepSeek-V4 模型中，hcpost 片段包含多个小算子组合，适合通过 AutoFuse 进行融合优化。通过 @torch.compile 装饰对 hcpost 函数进行编译，可以显著提升其执行性能。 python @torch.compile def hcpost(x: torch.Tensor, residual: torch.Tensor, post: torch.Tensor, comb:torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: y = post.unsqueeze(-1) x.unsqueeze(-2) + torch.sum(comb.unsqueeze(-1) residual.unsqueeze(-2), dim=2) return y.typeas(x) 性能数据在昇腾 A3 ，基于 hcpost 执行时的典型输入 shape 进行测试。 模型部分 未编译耗时 编译后耗时(dynamic=False) 性能提升 编译后耗时(dynamic=True) 性能提升 -------- ---------- ------------------------- -------- ------------------------ -------- hcpost 30 us 7.5 us 4x 10 us 3x AutoFuse JIT的算子生成能力 算子的核心交付件主要包含kernel源码与tiling源码，AutoFuse模块将算子代码的生成过程抽象为几个阶段： 1. AscendLoopIR是抽象算子计算过程的表达IR，描述计算过程、切分轴、UB内存等信息； 2. schedule组件负责对Hint graph进行处理。根据实际硬件的能力，提供能够应对所有shape场景的，全量的轴切分策略。每一个具体的切分策略由一张称为impl graph的AscendLoopIR承载，组合成一组impl graphs作为后续ATT与codegen组件的输入； 3. ATT组件负责根据每个impl graph生成tiling代码，tiling代码在执行时会根据具体shape评估每个impl graph对应kernel模板的性能，选择最优模板，计算切分参数，通过tilingdata传递给kernel； 4. codegen组件负责根据每个impl graph生成kernel代码，每个impl graph对应一份模板实现，在执行时根据tilingdata参数决定实际要执行的模板，以及循环搬入的具体参数； AutoFuse模块的源码已开源， 可在此获取 亲和NPU，模板规约的schedule技术 在NPU上，硬件单元一次运行，可以完成批数据的向量运算，为了充分发挥硬件特点，需要准确选择进行向量运算的轴。同时面对硬件的多核能力以及内存有限的状态，还需要进一步选择进行分核切分的轴、进行UB切分的轴。这三种轴的正确选择对功能与执行性能都有巨大影响，选择错误就容易出现UB超载的功能问题或性能严重劣化的问题。 不同的输入shape规格通常亲和不同的切分策略，特定切分策略的算子实现我们通常称为模板。提供通用的模板可以简化问题复杂度，但无法提供更好的性能效果；提供精细、繁多的模板库，可以面对不同场景提供极致性能，但会让模板选择、代码维护变得困难。 AutoFuse作为JIT的算子融合技术，在模板设计上选择了折中的方案，提供多模板，但对适用场景做抽象规约，控制模板数量。通过有限的模板数，在绝大多数shape规格下都能提供优秀的性能。Schedule模块负责根据HintGraph产生一组ImplGraph，每个ImplGraph对应一个模板实现。 以reduce多模板举例 Reduce融合是深度学习中最常见的场景之一，涉及Sum、Max、Min、Mean、Prod、Any、All等归约操作。其核心挑战在于： 归约轴与非归约轴的差异化处理 多核负载均衡 归约后的继续计算优化 为应对不同shape下的切分策略，归纳如下三类主要模板应对不同的适用场景。 模板类型 触发条件 调度特点 适用场景 --------------------- ----------------------------- ---------------------- -------------------- 全载模板 Reduce后节点≤4且为AR/ARA模式 不需要切分Reduce轴 小数据量、简单图结构 通用模板 默认选择 UB切分+Block切分 中等规模、通用场景 R轴分核模板 数据规模大且可切分 Reduce轴作为多核切分轴 Reduce轴较大 在大R轴场景，若只设计通用模板，会导致UB超载的功能问题；在小数据场景选择通用模板，则又会因为核启动开销大而影响性能； AutoSchedule实现介绍 AutoSchedule的核心思想是将融合图中的各种计算节点抽象为几大类ComputeType，根据每种类型在NPU上的特定切分方式，通过AxisGroup对轴进行语义分组，并利用Merge规则生成适用于所有节点的公共AxisGroup，最终生成多种切分候选方案（TilingCase）。 ComputeType抽象与NPU切分方式 将融合图中的各种计算节点抽象为几大类ComputeType，每种类型在NPU上有其特定的最优切分方式： ComputeType 典型算子 NPU切分特点 轴分组特征 --------------------- ---------------- -------------------------- ---------------------- Elementwise Add, Mul, Relu等 可任意维度切分，支持向量化 全部归入Y组 Broadcast 广播算子 需处理不同shape的对齐 计算轴归入Y组 Reduce Sum, Max, Min等 归约轴需特殊处理 归约轴R组，非归约轴Y组 Concat 拼接 拼接维度不能切分 非拼接轴归入Y组 AxisGroup轴分组与Merge规则 针对不同ComputeType的切分需求，定义了AxisGroup结构对轴进行语义分组： X组：需要完整数据的轴（如Concat拼接轴），切分后需保持数据完整性 Y组：元算子计算轴（如Elementwise），可灵活进行UB切分 R组：Reduce归约轴，采用专用的多核归约策略 由于融合图中可能包含多种ComputeType，通过Merge规则生成一个适用于所有节点的公共AxisGroup： 规则类型 合并条件 结果 说明 -------- ------------- ---------- ------------------------ Y+Y 两节点均为Y组 保持Y组 计算特性相同，可直接合并 Y+R Y组遇到R组 升级为R组 Reduce优先级更高 Y+YR Y组遇到YR组 扩展为YR组 兼容归约和非归约计算 TilingCase候选方案生成 基于公共AxisGroup，生成多种切分候选方案（TilingCase）。每个TilingCase定义了一组具体的切分参数： UB切分：指定哪个轴进行UB缓冲区切分 Block切分：指定哪个轴用于多核并行 Reduce特殊处理：是否启用R轴切多核策略 Schedule调度变换 Schedule对每个TilingCase执行具体的调度变换，将抽象的切分方案转换为具体的调度操作： 变换类型 说明 效果 --------------------------- -------------- ------------------------ TileSplit UB级切分 将数据分块加载到UB缓冲区 BlockSplit Block级切分 实现多核并行 ReduceBlockTiling Reduce专用切分 优化归约操作的多核执行 向量化 识别可向量化轴 提升计算吞吐 基于硬件建模，动态求解的算子tiling技术 schedule技术在编译时给出了应对不同shape的规约模板集合，在执行时就需要有配套技术能够正确选择模板，输出核切分，UB切分结果。计算结果错误会直接导致UB越界错误或性能急剧劣化。 在AutoFuse组件，此工作由ATT(Auto tiling)技术来完成。通过预置的性能建模以及多样的求解策略，来保证泛化场景的功能正确性与普适性能，同时寻求求解准度与求解速度之间的平衡。 自动Tiling的挑战 1. 性能评估的困难：schedule输出的不同模板，在 GM非连续性、UB非连续性、是否向量化宽度对齐、循环次数、计算瓶颈和 搬运瓶颈等方面存在较大差异，因此在不同的融合场景和Shape下会表现出不同的性能优劣。这就要求自动Tiling能够准确地评估不同模板的执行性能。 2. 分核与分块的权衡：增加分核数量会带来额外的 核启动开销（包括硬件开销和软件开销），而减少分核则会导致单核负荷过大。因此，如何合理权衡 分核数和 分Tile块大小成为我们面临的关键难题。 自动Tiling核心功能 自动Tiling的目标是找到能够实现 Kernel最佳执行性能的Tiling策略，其核心功能包括： 1. 寻找最优切分结果：为每个ImplGraph找到其最优切分结果，确定Kernel执行时需要使用的核数量、每次从GM搬运到UB的数据量、UB内的循环次数、每次UB内计算的数据量，以及每次从UB搬运到GM的次数； 2. 选出最优模板：基于每个ImplGraph的最优切分方案，尽可能准确地评估其Kernel执行性能，从而 选出最优模板。 自动Tiling核心流程 Kernel的执行逻辑会在IR中表达。自动Tiling会根据IR图的表达提取关键信息，包括： 约束的符号化表达: LocalBuffer占用约束：自动Tiling求解时需确保每一级LocalBuffer的占用都在硬件允许的范围内。例如，Kernel申请的TQue/TBuf及临时Buf的大小之和不能超过硬件的UB大小限制。IR会表达出每个Tensor的location（是在GM还是UB上）以及Tensor间的复用关系，自动Tiling根据这些信息将各级LocalBuffer的约束进行符号化表达。 核数占用约束：自动Tiling会根据轴的切分方式生成实际核数的符号化表达，在Tiling运行时根据实际的硬件约束和确定的符号值判断是否满足约束。 切分约束：例如，保证子轴大小小于等于父轴的约束、切分轴需要32B对齐等。 各流水耗时符号化表达 自动Tiling会对各个API进行 性能建模，通过 符号化的形式表达这些API在各个流水线上的性能。根据IR表达的循环轴来确定API的调用次数，从而推导出该IR的所有API在各个流水线上的总耗时。此处假设瓶颈流水线的执行可以较好地掩盖非瓶颈流水线的执行（瓶颈流水线简化理论），因此任务执行的总耗时主要体现在瓶颈流水线的时间上。如下图所示，图中包含三个pipe流水，其中瓶颈流水为AIVMTE2，AIVMTE2在执行时会掩盖AIVMTE3和AIVVEC的执行，任务执行的总耗时体现在AIVMTE2的执行耗时上。 pipe流水示意图 自动Tiling根据提取的关键信息生成Tiling求解器代码，默认生成 轴排序Tiling求解器。该求解器会以"算子实现过程中的存储占用不超过NPU各级物理存储大小"为约束条件，根据不同的IR表达，选择最合适的Tiling算法，保证基础解的性能；再以"最小化瓶颈执行单元的耗时"为优化目标，通过性能建模进行求解，提升解的性能上限。 此外，系统还提供可选配置的 启发式迭代求解器。该求解器采用启发式求解方法，从初始解开始，在满足约束条件的可行域内，沿着性能公式建模的梯度下降方向搜索满足内存要求的解空间，直到公式建模的值达到最小值时退出寻优流程，并返回最优Tiling。 关键技术 性能公式建模： 定位：性能公式的仿真精度决定了： 对Schedule生成的模板选择的准确性； 轴排序核数调整及核内循环选择的准确性； 启发式迭代求解的准确性。 因此，需要对各类API进行尽可能精确的性能建模。 搬运类API建模实现： 1. 识别影响搬运性能的主要因素。 例如：数据量、GM非连续性、UB非连续性、是否向量化宽度对齐、分核数、Pipe头开销、API头开销、API调用次数等。 2. 基于影响搬运性能的主要因素及其对性能的影响，设计性能公式。 例如，假设MTE2的开销为Cost(MTE2)，其中 API头开销为h，数据量为DataSize，API调用次数为Count，Pipe头开销为H，带宽为T： Cost(MTE2) = ((DataSize / T + h) Count) + H 其中 带宽是与 是否向量化宽度对齐、分核数、GM非连续性、UB非连续性相关的因变量。 3. 基于假设的性能模型，通过实验验证不同主因素变化下的实际搬运性能。 4. 建立搬运性能与主因素之间的关系，并通过符号化技术表达出来。 计算类API建模实现： 1. 针对AscendC的 稳定基础API，自动Tiling模块会根据不同的输入采集性能数据，得到 性能与输入的关系，并建立性能模型，通过符号化技术表达出来。 2. 针对调用AscendC的 易变API，自动Tiling模块会基于 API调用的逻辑，计算其 调用入参和 调用次数，生成该API的完整性能模型，从而得到相对准确的性能建模。 基于 搬运类API建模和 计算类API建模，以及 瓶颈流水线简化理论，可以将自动Tiling的两个核心问题简化为： 1. 如何调整Tiling使得瓶颈流水公式值最小； 2. 选择瓶颈流水公式值最小的模板作为最优模板。 轴排序求解器： 定位： Tiling求解器的目标是基于输入Shape确定合适的分核及分块大小，以获得尽可能好的Kernel性能。轴排序求解器支持的启发式优先级排序规则（优先是指优先不切的轴）及基础算法（如 UB占用核数占用权衡算法、UB优先贪心算法、对称切分）可以很好地保证基础解的性能，另一方面结合性能建模的表达可以提升Kernel性能的上限。 实现： 确定切分轴的优先级：首先需要基于API来确定切分轴的 优先级，顺序如下： 父轴优先级高于子轴（功能性硬约束）； 规约化类轴高于非规约化类轴（启发式规则）； 广播轴高于非广播轴（启发式规则）； 非最内轴高于最内轴（启发式规则）； 搬运API的尾轴具有同等优先级（启发式规则）。 分核与核内切分：其次分成两个部分进行切分，包括 核内Tiling和 分核Tiling。以 UB优先贪心算法为例（适合API头开销较大的场景）： 核内Tiling：按照轴排序的逆序依次遍历，优先将变量调整至最大值，判断是否符合硬件约束条件。若不满足，则通过二分法调整该变量，直到符合硬件约束条件为止，随后调整下一个核内Tiling变量，直至所有变量均满足硬件约束条件。例如，s1tt2、s1tt、s1t、s2t是Tiling相关轴，其切分流程如下： 分核Tiling：识别与多核相关的变量，按从大到小的顺序遍历这些变量，找到核数占用更大的记录，若超出物理核数则返回。如下图所示，bngs1T是多核切分轴，其切分流程如下。选择策略为：当核数占用不同时，优先选择占用核数更大的记录。根据上述策略，最终选定的占用核数为47。 具体流程为：优先遍历s2t，调至最大值1024，符合硬件约束条件；然后遍历s1t，调至最大值256，符合硬件约束条件；然后依次调整下个变量s1tt>s1tt2，直到所有变量均满足硬件约束条件。 其他算法： UB占用核数占用权衡算法：适合需要精细控制核数占用及UB占用的场景（有预设值，可根据性能公式动态调整核数）。 对称切分：适合尾轴转置场景，需要保证作为搬运类API的多个尾轴可以按照同等优先级切分。 基于AscendLoopIR表达的，AscendC算子kernel代码生成能力
