If HiF8 is later extended to more operators suitable for low-bit quantization, there is still room for further improvement in the overall benefits. 6.1 Source of HiF8's Benefits over BF16 Compared with BF16, the performance gain of HiF8 mainly comes from the memory-access benefits brought by the reduced data bit width, as well as the throughput advantages of the low-bit computation path. 6.1.1 Memory-Access Benefits from Halving the Data Bit Width When the data bit width is reduced from 16-bit BF16 to 8-bit HiF8, the data movement volume of the inputs, outputs, and intermediate activations of matrix-multiplication-related operators decreases accordingly. In large-model training, some operators are often limited by memory bandwidth, so halving the bit width can usually bring the following benefits: Reduced on-chip memory bandwidth pressure: The amount of data transferred per unit time decreases, thereby easing the read/write pressure on the high-bandwidth on-chip memory; Improved on-chip cache utilization: With the same on-chip SRAM / Cache capacity, more data can be accommodated, which helps improve the data reuse rate; Reduced data movement latency: The data transfer overhead between different storage levels, such as from on-chip memory to registers, decreases, thereby shortening the waiting time in non-compute stages. 6.1.2 The Throughput-Improving Effect of 8-bit Computation In addition to the memory-access benefits, HiF8 can also exploit the higher throughput that the underlying hardware provides for low-bit matrix operations. Current AI acceleration hardware is usually specifically optimized for the 8-bit computation path, so when backbone operators such as MM and GMM are mapped to the HiF8 path, compute utilization can be further improved and translated into training speed gains. As shown in Figure 13, the average speedup of HiF8 over BF16 for the MM and GMM operators exceeds 1.8x. Figure 13: Comparison schematic of the MM operator (left) and GMM operator (right) for HiF8 vs. BF16 6.2 Source of HiF8's Benefits over MXFP8 Compared with MXFP8, the additional benefits of HiF8 are mainly related to the quantization granularity and the scaling metadata overhead. In the trimmed DeepSeek-V3 network, the profiling comparison of the GMM operator under the HiF8 and MXFP8 quantization schemes is shown in Figure 14. Combined with the experimental results, the advantages of HiF8 over MXFP8 can be summarized into the following three aspects. Figure 14: Profiling comparison schematic of the GMM quantization operator for HiF8 vs. MXFP8 6.2.1 Lower Scaling Metadata Overhead MXFP8 usually adopts Per-Block fine-grained quantization, which requires maintaining additional scaling factors for each data block and frequently accessing this metadata during computation. In contrast, because HiF8 has a larger dynamic range, it can usually adopt Per-Tensor quantization, thereby reducing the number of scaling factors and their memory-access overhead. The corresponding benefits mainly include: Fewer load and store operations for scaling factors; Reduced extra memory overhead for storing fine-grained Scale; More contiguous data access patterns, reducing alignment and access issues caused by fragmented metadata. 6.2.2 Relatively Simple Control Logic Per-Block quantization requires the operator to handle logic such as block boundary switching, local dequantization, and cross-block Scale alignment during execution, which increases control complexity and affects operator fusion and pipelined execution. In contrast, when HiF8 adopts the Per-Tensor path, the internal data flow of the operator is more contiguous and the related control logic is simpler, making it easier to achieve stable execution efficiency. 6.2.3 More Suitable for Delayed Scaling Training HiF8 has a larger dynamic range, so during training it can adopt Delayed Scaling with a lower update frequency without significantly affecting training stability. This gives it certain advantages in the following aspects: Lower frequency of Amax statistics; Reduced Scale updates and related synchronization operations; Less interference with the main computation flow. In contrast, FP8 / MXFP8 with smaller dynamic ranges often need to update scaling parameters more frequently, or rely on finer-grained scaling strategies, which adds extra control overhead. 6.3 Current Conclusions and Future Optimization Space Judging from the current experimental results, HiF8 shows good application potential in large-model training scenarios. On the one hand, under the existing experimental configuration, the loss curve and gradient norm of HiF8 are essentially aligned with those of BF16, indicating that it can maintain good training stability on the current task. On the other hand, in terms of end-to-end performance, HiF8 is superior to both BF16 and MXFP8, indicating that it achieves a good balance among numerical range, quantization granularity, and system overhead. From an implementation perspective, HiF8 has a low dependence on fine-grained scaling and large amounts of metadata, which helps reduce the complexity of operator implementation and facilitates subsequent scaling to larger-scale training tasks. Future work can continue in the following directions: Expanding operator coverage: Extending HiF8 quantization to more operators suitable for low-bit conversion, such as FlashAttention (FA) and related collective communication operators; Optimizing the scaling update mechanism: Further researching Amax statistics and Scale update strategies better suited to HiF8, so as to reduce extra overhead and improve numerical stability; Carrying out software-hardware co-optimization: Combining compiler and underlying hardware instruction capabilities to further optimize the low-bit data path and operator fusion implementations. Chapter 7 Recommended Scheme and Implementation Guide Based on the aforementioned format design, quantization approaches, and analysis of experimental results, this document summarizes a set of recommended configurations suitable for large-scale neural network training. 7.1 Recommended Configuration for HiF8 Training While balancing training precision and system throughput, the recommended configuration is shown in Table 7. Table 7: Recommended configuration for HiF8 training Configuration dimension Recommended scheme Core motivation - - - Quantization granularity Per-tensor Maximizes the advantages of the HiF8 format and eliminates the memory-access and control burden brought by Per-block. Scaling strategy Delayed Scaling Reduces the metadata overhead and control complexity caused by Per-Block quantization Update interval Interval = 10 steps Leverages the dynamic range advantage of HiF8 to reduce the update frequency of scaling parameters Operators covered MM / GMM Prioritizes covering compute-intensive backbone operators Master Weights FP32 / BF16 Ensures numerical precision during the parameter update stage When the model and task allow, it is recommended to prioritize Per-Tensor quantization to reduce Scale metadata overhead and implementation complexity. For the scaling strategy, it is recommended to prioritize Delayed Scaling and set the update interval to 10 steps or higher to reduce statistics and synchronization overhead. For the quantization coverage, one can start with compute-intensive operators such as MM and GMM, and then gradually expand to other operators suitable for low-bit conversion. 7.2 Core Scheme Optimization Recommendations When implementing the above scheme, it is recommended to follow the following principles to balance training precision, system efficiency, and implementation complexity. Prioritize Per-Tensor quantization. Because HiF8 has a large dynamic range, Per-Tensor quantization can usually already meet the precision requirements in most LLM training scenarios. Compared with fine-grained quantization, this approach can significantly reduce the storage and access overhead of Scale metadata, and reduce memory-access fragmentation and control complexity. Prioritize Delayed Scaling. It is recommended to combine the numerical range advantage of HiF8, adopt the Delayed Scaling strategy with a lower update frequency, and set the update interval to 10 steps or higher. This can reduce the extra overhead caused by Amax statistics, Scale updates, and related synchronization operations, which is beneficial for improving the continuity of the main computation flow. Evaluate the scheme comprehensively from the three aspects of numerical capability, training stability, and system overhead. Through the Dot field, redundancy-free exponent encoding, and Denormal extension, HiF8 provides a large dynamic range at 8-bit width; under the experimental setting in this document, its loss curve and gradient statistics are essentially aligned with those of BF16, demonstrating good training stability; at the same time, HiF8 supports coarser-grained quantization and longer-interval scaling updates, which helps reduce metadata access and control logic overhead and achieve good end-to-end performance benefits. 7.3 Summary This document analyzes the data format design, quantization scheme, training framework support, and experimental results of HiF8. The experiments show that, on the 950DT platform and the trimmed DeepSeek-V3 model, HiF8 achieves a 29.5% end-to-end training speedup over BF16 while maintaining training precision similar to BF16, and obtains an 11.3% performance improvement over MXFP8. Judging from the current results, HiF8 achieves a good balance among numerical range, training stability, and system overhead. For large-model training scenarios that seek to reduce memory-access pressure, improve training throughput, and control implementation complexity, HiF8 is an 8-bit mixed-precision training scheme with engineering application value. In the future, a HiF8 pretraining example based on the trimmed DeepSeek-V3 model will be added to the cann-recipes-train open-source repository for subsequent validation and reproduction.

CANN + TorchTitan: Ascend Optimization Practice for DeepSeek-V3.2 32k Long-Sequence Pretraining With the release of DeepSeek-V3.2 by the DeepSeek team, its innovative DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) architecture has significantly improved long-sequence computation efficiency through the sparse attention mechanism, quickly becoming the focus of industry attention. To seize this technology trend, many vendors are eager to quickly complete the adaptation and reproduction of DSA and integrate it into their own models to explore performance benefits, which also poses a challenge to the rapid adaptation of training frameworks on Ascend NPUs. This document mainly introduces the technical practice of achieving full-pipeline pretraining adaptation of DeepSeek-V3.2 on Ascend NPU clusters using the PyTorch official native large-model training framework TorchTitan. We not only worked through the complex hybrid parallel strategies, but also took the industry lead in overcoming the backward propagation challenge of the DSA operator. Combined with torch.compile compilation acceleration, we achieved native alignment from model definition to operator compilation. The DeepSeek-V3.2 long-sequence CPT training reproduced by the CANN team achieves a performance of 148 TPS/card in the extreme memory scenario on an A3 64-card cluster. -- Highlights The training framework uses the TorchTitan + TorchTitan-npu plug-in scheme. The parallel strategies enable native TP/PP/EP/FSDP2 Ascend adaptation, and a Custom CP is proposed for the sparse DSA structure. 32K long-sequence CPT training is completed on an A3 64-card cluster, and the involved training framework code has been fully open-sourced Based on Ascend C, we implement NPU fused forward and backward Kernels for Lightning Indexer and Sparse Flash Attention, unleashing the potential of sparse computation. The Ascend C Kernel technical documentation and code have been open-sourced Leveraging the native memory advantages of FSDP2 (Fully Sharded Data Parallel 2), combined with the high communication bandwidth hardware characteristics of the A3 super node, the weight prefetch communication can be fully masked by computation; at the same time, by taking advantage of the A3 high-speed H2D bandwidth to enable Swap Optimizer to Host memory, a memory minimal deployment scheme for 671B long-sequence full fine-tuning is achieved TorchTitan-npu seamlessly interfaces with the torch.compile + Inductor graph optimization capabilities to implement FX computation graph pass optimization, achieving performance gains in the DeepSeek-V3.2 pretraining scenario, and is the main battlefield for future PyTorch compilation optimization in training scenarios Outline Why Choose TorchTitan Distributed Parallelism Strategies Memory Optimization DSA Fused Operators FSDP2 + Torch.compile + Inductor Acceleration Benchmark Future Plan Why Choose TorchTitan Native Distributed Programming Model The most fundamental advantage of TorchTitan lies in its deep application of DTensor, which abstracts tensor parallelism as first-class semantics and enables Lego-style combination of parallel strategies. Unified abstraction: DTensor decouples parameter partitioning from model definition through Placement (Shard/Replicate/Partial). Developers only need to configure the ParallelStyle of submodules to declare the partitioning approach, without explicitly writing communication logic. Multi-dimensional combination: Based on DTensor carrying the complete device mesh, TorchTitan can implement 5D parallel (FSDP2+TP+PP+EP+CP) combinations at extremely low intrusion cost, keeping the codebase compact and modular while supporting rich features. Seamless Integration with the PyTorch Ecosystem TorchTitan is a native large-model training framework of the PyTorch community. Integrating with TorchTitan helps accelerate the deep integration of the Ascend ecosystem with the PyTorch community, reuse open-source solutions, and effectively improve the ease of use of NPU training scenarios. Deep Integration of torch.compile TorchTitan natively supports torch.compile and leverages the Inductor compiler to achieve training optimization: FX graph transformation: Captures the static graph through FX, executes graph-level passes such as computation scheduling and pattern matching, automatically eliminates redundant operations, and generates a streamlined intermediate representation. Operator fusion: Relies on Triton to implement horizontal fusion (merging chains of consecutive elementwise operations) and vertical fusion (merging compute-intensive operators with bias, activations, etc.), reducing memory access and kernel launch overhead. In the future, the CANN platform can connect to Inductor through Ascend C automatic fusion to further improve performance. Integration of Native PyTorch Community Tools TorchTitan integrates the tool systems in the PyTorch ecosystem, providing out-of-the-box stability and debugging capabilities: Distributed checkpointing: Natively integrates DCP and supports asynchronous saving; CheckpointManager saves model shards, optimizer states, and loader offsets at low overhead, and automatically locates the latest checkpoint and verifies its integrity upon recovery. Fault tolerance and diagnostics: TorchFT enables replica-level checkpoint management. In HSDP scenarios, only the failed node can be recovered upon node failure, significantly improving the mean time between failures; based on FlightRecorder, information such as communication types, data volumes, and call stacks can be cached to assist in locating the root causes of deadlocks and training timeouts. Low-precision training: Pluggable integration of TorchAO reuses its low-precision data type abstractions and quantization recipes. The community has implemented support for FP8 / MxFP8 data types in TorchTitan and completed validation of low-precision MoE network training. TorchTitan-npu Pluggable Support Scheme TorchTitan provides the ModelConverter mechanism, which acts after the model definition and before the application of parallel strategies (TP/FSDP, etc.). It can replace or rewrite model modules through a registration mechanism without modifying the original model definition. For details, please refer to the official documentation Based on this mechanism, we designed an NPU pluggable adaptation scheme, with the expected goals: Do not modify upstream model code, making it easy to track upstream updates Support enabling optimization items through switches Support free combination of multiple optimization items Currently, we mainly enable fused operator optimization, while features such as quantization and optimizer optimization are being gradually expanded; this mechanism also makes it convenient to combine with capabilities such as torch.compile to achieve further optimization. Usage example: yaml [model] # Simply specify the fused operators to be enabled under the [model] configuration converters = ["npudsa", "npurmsnorm", "npupermute", "npugmm"] Distributed Parallelism Strategies: MoE TP Strategy Optimization In the large-EP scenario, routed experts are not partitioned by TP (TP extend EP). The native MoE TP strategy of TorchTitan is shown in the following figure: The above strategy has unreasonable aspects in both branches: The routed expert branch receives the activation tensor after AllGather in the TP domain. Every rank within a TP domain performs topk selection on the same tensor, causing redundancy in computation and memory; at the same time, the Reorder module also performs Sequence Parallel, which means the preceding TP-domain AllGather is a redundant operation for the routed expert branch. Unlike traditional TP, the shared expert branch does not immediately perform ReduceScatter communication on its output; instead, it maintains an unsafe Partial state and occupies more memory. The above unreasonable aspects are related to the unreasonable placement of AllGather and ReduceScatter in the TP domain. These two communication operations can be moved to the shared expert branch, while the routed expert branch does not need TP-domain communication. After the adjustment, the MoE TP strategy is shown in the following figure: the routed expert branch no longer has redundant computation and communication, and the shared expert branch follows the ordinary TP strategy: Custom CP Strategy Introduction to Native torch CP In long-sequence scenarios, Context Parallel (CP) over the Sequence dimension of input data is particularly important, as it can greatly reduce the activation memory footprint. TorchTitan uses the context parallel capability natively provided by torch. Its principle is shown in the following figure: a context environment wraps the model training step. Inside the context, the model input is partitioned along the sequence axis, and the Attention operator is replaced with a RingAttention or AllGatherKV implementation to ensure correct Attention computation. Custom CP for DSA Unlike traditional dense attention models, the internal Lightning Indexer and DSA sparse attention of the DeepSeek-V3.2 model both need to process Key and Value in the CP scenario to ensure computational correctness. Since the internal attention structure of DeepSeek-V3.2 is more complex and the Attention operator is no longer the commonly used SDPA, the native CP capability of torch does not apply. In this context, while following the design logic of native torch CP, we designed and implemented a custom CP for DeepSeek-V3.2, whose principle is shown in the following figure: In the CP scenario, it is necessary to ensure that qindexer and query each perform attention computation with the kindexer and key value of the full sequence. Generally, there are two ways to achieve this: the RingAttention form, or directly performing AllGather on KV along the sequence dimension. RingAttention form: Complex to implement, and it needs to be implemented for both the Indexer and the sparse attention computation; overall, it is complex to develop and not flexible enough. Performing sequence-dimension AllGather on KV: Simple and flexible to implement. In addition, considering that under weight absorb mode, KV occupies little memory and the key in the Indexer also occupies very little memory, the memory cost of AllGather is fully acceptable. Based on the above analysis, we implemented a CP version of the DSA forward function, which simply adds AllGather communication for KV on top of the original code. Taking the DSA implementation using NPU fused operators as an example, the computation logic in the CP scenario is shown in the following figure: It is worth mentioning that we first implemented the CustomContextParallelContext base class, which only performs sequence partitioning of the model input. Users can customize the CP patch logic of the model forward computation in subclasses, providing good extensibility. Sharding Strategy Optimization for DTensor Computation Operator Sharding Strategies When using DTensor for computation, the operator dispatch needs to generate sharding strategies for the operator's inputs (including weights) and outputs. For a DTensor, if the selected sharding strategy does not match the current state, it triggers a DTensor state transition, introducing extra operations such as Slice or communication, which can have a very adverse impact on performance and even memory. Therefore, generating a reasonable sharding strategy for operators is crucial. This subsection introduces the sharding strategy optimization for two NPU operators. Matmul Sharding Strategy Optimization In the TP scenario, the current default matmul sharding strategy generation is unreasonable. Taking the qlora matrix multiplication as an example, this matrix multiplication does not perform any partitioning within the TP domain, so the matmul can be computed directly, as shown on the right side of the following figure. However, the current sharding strategy generation is unreasonable. As shown on the left side of the following figure, the generated strategy tries to turn the simple Replicate matrix multiplication into a form where the weight is partitioned along the TP rows, introducing many extra operations and greatly affecting performance: Input X: Changes from Replicate to Shard(2), requiring a Slice operation. Weight W: Changes from Replicate to Shard(0), requiring a Slice operation. Output Y: Since the TP strategy specifies that the qlora module is not parallelized, the final matmul output needs to be adjusted to the Replicate state, and transitioning from Partial to Replicate requires AllReduce communication. In fact, PyTorch has already written a fairly complete matmul sharding strategy generation function, which can be used to obtain a more reasonable sharding strategy. For the above example, the expected reasonable strategy can be obtained through the following code: Matmul Backward Sharding Strategy Optimization The matmulbackward operator also currently has the problem of unreasonable sharding strategies. Taking the output matrix multiplication at the end of the model as an example, its forward pass uses the weight partitioned along the TP columns. In the backward pass, the input partitioning state and the generated default partitioning strategy are shown on the left side of the following figure, and the unreasonable strategy introduces redundant operations: Input X: Changes from Replicate to Shard(2), requiring a Slice operation. Gradient dY: Changes from Shard(2) to Replicate, requiring AllGather communication and occupying more memory. Weight W: Changes from Shard(1) to Shard(0), requiring AllToAll communication. Although torch does not have a sharding strategy generation function for matmul backward, considering that matmul backward is essentially two matrix multiplications that compute dX and dW, we designed to call mmlikestrategy for the two matrix multiplications separately to generate strategies, and then fuse them to obtain the final matmul backward sharding strategy. In addition, since mmlikestrategy generates multiple strategies for a single matmul, it is also necessary to consider how to select a more reasonable strategy. Since the weight partitioning state is usually not adjusted again during computation, we select, from among the many strategies, the strategy that does not adjust the partitioning state of W (for the dX computation) and the strategy where dW is consistent with the partitioning state of W (for the dW computation). Fusing the two strategies yields the ideal strategy on the right side of the above figure. It can be seen that the ideal strategy actually does not adjust the partitioning state of the operator's input tensor, thereby avoiding the introduction of extra operations. Memory Optimization Minimal Partitioning Strategy The core challenge of this deployment is to deploy the DeepSeek-V3.2 model training task, whose parameter count is as high as 671B, on a small-scale A3 cluster of 64 cards. Considering that TorchTitan currently stores model weights using the FP32 type, the weights and gradients of DeepSeek-V3.2 occupy 5368GB, exceeding the total memory of 4096GB on 32 A3 cards. Therefore, 64 cards is already the smallest possible scale for model deployment. Under this constraint, the deployment strategy needs to center on the main thread of 'extremely compressing per-card memory usage'. FSDP2 Flow and Characteristics FSDP2, as the core evolutionary scheme of PyTorch distributed training, has a core flow that, at each computation step (forward/backward), collects on demand the full set of model parameters partitioned across devices via AllGather, and immediately releases parameters not on the local device after computation completes, thereby reducing the resident memory associated with model parameters and gradients. Compared with FSDP1, FSDP2 has deeply optimized sharding granularity, communication overlap, and memory reuse: it supports unified shard management of parameters, gradients, and optimizer states; it adopts a layer-wise collection and release mechanism to achieve an efficient pipeline where communication and computation mask each other; and it natively adapts to mixed-precision training and the automated partitioning configuration of the TorchTitan framework. Zero-Redundancy Weights In the common large-EP, small-TP deployment mode of MoE models, although the MoE part, which accounts for the majority of the model's parameters, is fully partitioned through EP and pipeline parallelism (PP) with expert weights scattered without redundancy, the weights of the Attention/shared-expert parts are often redundantly replicated across cards. In such scenarios where hybrid parallel strategies cause partial parameter redundancy, the advantage of FSDP2 is particularly prominent: by further partitioning the redundantly deployed Attention weights and shared-expert parameters in DP-domain units, FSDP2 can significantly reduce the number of parameter copies across DP domains while keeping the computation logic unchanged, freeing valuable resources for larger-batch or longer-sequence training. Specifically, considering the PP2TP4DP16 scenario, the total per-card occupancy of non-MoE weights and gradients is approximately (671B - 654B)/PP2/TP4 8Byte = 18GB. Considering that some of these weights do not participate in TP partitioning (such as qkva and indexer), the actual value will increase further. After enabling FSDP in the DP16 scenario, the weights and gradients are fully and evenly divided among DP domains, almost completely eliminating the related memory usage. Finally, we compared the following partitioning strategies and, after considering the possibility of extreme MoE load imbalance, chose the partitioning approach based on PP2TP4EP64. Swap Optimizer The AdamW optimizer commonly used in large-model training needs to store two FP32 momentum values, which brings a huge memory cost: during the forward and backward computation of training, the optimizer is not used, so the optimizer wastes a massive amount of device memory. To address this problem, the MindSpeed open-source training framework designed the SwapOptimizer feature (Chinese) , which optimizes memory in the following ways: To save device memory, the optimizer is offloaded to host memory during the forward and backward passes. To reduce the memory peak during optimizer updates and improve performance as much as possible, "optimizer load — optimizer update — optimizer offload" is designed in a sliced, pipelined, and parallel form at the param granularity. This example references and implements the SwapOptimizer feature under the TorchTitan framework, greatly saving device memory during training. Unlike MindSpeed, in TorchTitan training the optimizer only manages two FP32 momentum values, and it also needs to handle the scenario where weights are DTensors. DSA Fused Operators LI/SFA For an introduction to the LightningIndexer/SparseFlashAttention related operators, please refer to NPU DeepSeek-V3.2 Ascend C Fused Operator Optimization SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss obtains the backward gradient computation for the Top-$k$ positions corresponding to each token in the Sparse Training Stage through a series of operations, and fuses the Loss computation into it. The backward gradient computation process depends on the aggregation and normalization results of the softmax in the Sparse Flash Attention computation process and the output distribution of the Lightning Indexer itself. Considering the balance between memory and compute power, the SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss operator performs partial recomputation while retaining some important forward computation results. The forward inputs of the Lightning Indexer are Index Query $\tilde{Q}\in\R^{g\times d}$ and Index Key $\tilde{K}\in\R^{S{k}\times d}$; the forward inputs of Sparse Flash Attention are Query $Q\in\R^{g\times d}$, Key $K\in\R^{S{k}\times d}$, and $W\in\R^{g\times 1}$, where $g$ is the group size corresponding to GQA, $d$ is the dimension of each head, and $S{k}$ is the context length. The specific computation flow of the SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss operator is as follows: 1. The computation formula for the forward Top-$k$ value of the Lightning Indexer: $$ {t,:}=W{t,:}@ReLU(\tilde{q}{t,:}@\tilde{K}{topk,:}^\top) $$ Here, $W{t,:}$ is the $weights$ corresponding to the $t$-th token in the $W$ matrix, $\tilde{q}{t,:}$ is the result after axis-merging the $G$ query heads corresponding to the $t$-th token in the $\tilde{Q}$ matrix, and $\tilde{K}{topk,:}$ is the matrix composed of tokens taken from the $\tilde{K}$ matrix according to the Top-$k$ indices of $\tilde{q}{t,:}$. 2. The computation formula for the forward Top-$k$ value of Sparse Flash Attention: $$ {t,:} = \text{Softmax}(q{t,:} @ K{topk,:}^\top/\sqrt{d}) $$ Here, $p{t,:}$ is the Softmax result corresponding to the $t$-th token, $q{t,:}$ is the result after axis-merging the $G$ query heads corresponding to the $t$-th token in the $Q$ matrix, and ${K}{topk,:}$ is the matrix composed of tokens taken from the $K$ matrix according to the Top-$k$ indices of ${q}{t,:}$. 3. During the training stage, the output of the Lightning Indexer needs to be aligned with the softmax result of Sparse Flash Attention to compute the loss. The corresponding loss function is: $$ oss{=}\sumtD{KL}(p{t,:}Softmax(I{t,:})) $$ Here, $p{t,:}$ serves as the target distribution, which needs to be obtained by summing over all heads on the previous computation results, and then applying L1 normalization to the summed result along the context direction. $D{KL}$ is the KL divergence, whose expression is: $$ D{KL}(ab){=}\sumiai\mathrm{log}{\left(\frac{ai}{bi}\right)} $$ 4. By taking the derivative, the gradient expression of the Loss can be obtained: $$ I\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{t,:}}=Softmax \left( I\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{t,:}} \left) -p\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{t,:}}\right. \right. $$ 5. Using the chain rule, the gradients of the weights, query, and key matrices can be computed: $$ W\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{t,:}}=dI\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{t,:}}\text{@} \left( ReLU \left( S\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{t,:}} \left) \left) \mathop{{}}\nolimits^{\top}\right. \right. \right. \right. $$ $$ \mathop{{\tilde{q}}}\nolimits{{t,:}}=dS\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{t,:}}@\tilde{K}{topk,:} $$ $$ \tilde{K}{topk,:}=\left(dS\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{t,:}} \left) \mathop{{}}\nolimits^{\top}@\tilde{q}\mathop{{}}\nolimits{{:t, :}}\right. \right. $$ Here, $S$ is the result of the matrix multiplication of $\tilde{Q}$ and $\tilde{K}$, and $S{t,:}$ is the $t$-th row in the $S$ matrix. $dW{t,:}$ is the $t$-th row in the $dW$ matrix; $dq{t,:}$ is the $t$-th row in the $d\tilde{Q}$ matrix; $d\tilde{K}{topk,:}$ is the accumulated value of the rows corresponding to the Top-$k$ indices in the $d\tilde{K}$ matrix. In actual development, it is necessary to fully exploit the characteristics of Ascend hardware to achieve better performance. The following will detail the current solutions and specific implementation approaches. SLIG Operator Tiling Design The inter-core Tiling design of the operator is as follows: SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss partitions the B and S axes across cores. The intra-core Tiling design of the operator is as follows: SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss uses a basic block size of $(128,128)$ for a single computation. The L1 space is divided as follows: $Q$ matrix: $128\times 576\times2\text{ Bytes}=144\text{ KB}$, i.e., the $Q$ matrix permanently resides in L1; $Qindex$ matrix with Double Buffer enabled: $2\times64\times 128\times2\text{ Bytes}=32\text{ KB}$, i.e., the $Qindex$ matrix permanently resides in L1; $Gather$ matrix with Double Buffer enabled: $2\times128\times 128\times2\text{ Bytes}=64\text{ KB}$, where the transfer size of the $Gather$ matrix each time is $(128,128)$; $reluGrad$ matrix: $64\times 2048\times2\text{ Bytes}=288\text{ KB}$, where the transfer size of the $reluGrad$ matrix each time is $(64,2048)$. L0A, L0B, and L0C have DoubleBuffer enabled and are divided into $2\times32\text{ KB}$, $2\times32\text{ KB}$, and $2\times64\text{ KB}$, respectively, In the $C1$ stage, the matrix block sizes loaded once into L0A and L0B by $MatmulP$ are $(128,128) / (128,64)$ and $(128,128)$, respectively. In the $C1$ stage, the matrix block sizes loaded once into L0A and L0B by $MatmulSy$ are $(64,128)$ and $(128,128)$, respectively. In the $C2$ stage, the matrix block sizes loaded once into L0A and L0B by $MatmulDk$ are $(128,64)$ and $(64,128)$, respectively. In the $C2$ stage, the matrix block sizes loaded once into L0A and L0B by $MatmulDq$ are $(64,128)$ and $(128,128)$, respectively. SLIG Pipeline Design The computation flow of SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss has five stages: preprocessing Gather ($V0$), matrix multiplication and ReLU operations ($C1$), followed by multiple vector computations on the $V1$ side, the $C1$-side matrix multiplications, and the post-processing ScatterAdd operation ($V2$). Compared with the LightningIndexer and SparseFlashAttention operators, the computation flow of this operator is more elaborate and its data dependencies are more complex. A naive pipeline arrangement causes a large number of bubbles in the Cube and Vector computation processes, failing to fully exploit the compute advantage. To prevent multiple stages from executing serially, it is necessary to Preload one $V0$ in advance to achieve mutual masking of the pipeline. The specific pipeline effect is shown in the following figure: Dispersed Memory-Access Optimization The Gather ($V0$) and ScatterAdd ($V2$) stages of the SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss operator both require dispersed memory access. For Attention operators in non-Sparse scenarios, data access is generally contiguous, so the time of a single data transfer is longer than the instruction dispatch time, enabling continuous multiple memory accesses and achieving high memory-access bandwidth. However, for the dispersed memory access of Sparse Attention, the time of a single memory access drops significantly, possibly even becoming shorter than the instruction dispatch time, which leads to severe instruction dispatch blocking, as shown in the following figure. Based on the characteristic of the A3 chip that the ratio of Cube cores to Vector cores is 1:2, the Vector cores are used to issue memory-access instructions, doubling the instruction dispatch efficiency. On the other hand, the amount of data in a single memory access itself also affects the actually achieved bandwidth, while a single dispersed memory access has a small access amount, which causes the data transfer time itself to be higher than expected. To address this problem, discrete data points can be aggregated in pairs, using the srcGap parameter to implement paired data access, thereby improving memory-access bandwidth, as shown in the figure. Axis-Merging Optimization Because different QueryTokens of the SparseLightningIndexerGradKLLoss operator correspond to different KeyTokens, the N axis is placed as the inner loop axis, and the B and S axes are used as the partitioning axes. SparseFlashAttentionGrad The SparseFlashAttention operator overall follows the computation flow of FlashAttentionGrad (Chinese) , with meticulous optimizations of instruction reduction and transfer aggregation for dispersed memory access. The backward computation is overall divided into the following core steps, and the overall computation logic is as follows: 1. Take out the corresponding tokens from the $K$ matrix according to the Top-$k$ indices to form the $K{topk}$ matrix. $$ {topk} = \text{Gather}(K, \text{Top-K index}) $$ 2. Recompute the forward softmax result of Sparse Flash Attention: $$ = \text{Softmax}(Q @ K{topk}^\top/\sqrt{d}) $$ 3. Perform matrix multiplication between $dY$ and the transposed $V$ matrix to obtain $dP$: $$ dP = dY @ V^T $$ 4. Subtract the FlashSoftmaxGrad computation result from $dP$, then multiply by $P$ to obtain $dS$: $$ dS = P (dP - \text{FlashSoftmaxGrad}(dY @ attention\in)) $$ Here, the inputs of FlashSoftmaxGrad are the backward gradient dY and the forward output attentionin. 5. Using the chain rule, the gradients of the query, key, and value matrices can be computed: $$ dQ = dS @ K{topk} /\sqrt{d} $$ $$ dK = \text{ScatterAdd}(dS^\top @ Q /\sqrt{d},\text{Top-K index} ) $$ $$ dV = P^\top @ dY $$ SFAG Operator Tiling Design The Tiling design of an operator determines whether the storage space is fully utilized, which in turn affects the overall compute utilization and operator performance. For SparseFlashAttentionScoreGrad, this section describes the inter-core and intra-core Tiling designs respectively. The inter-core Tiling design adopts the following scheme: Currently, the SparseFlashAttentionScoreGrad operator merges the Batch axis with $S{Q}$ and uses it as the core-partitioning axis, with the cores arranged consecutively along the partitioning axis. T = B $S{Q}$ CoreProcessNum = CeilDiv(T, CoreNum) The intra-core Tiling design adopts the following scheme: Intra-core space partitioning: Left matrix L1 basic block Right matrix L1 basic block ------------------------- ------------------ ----------------- $Q{index}$ @ $K{index}$ 128 576 128 128 2(DB) $d{y}$ @V 128 512 128 128 2(DB) $d{s}$ @ K 128 128 2(DB) 128 128 2(DB) $d{s}$ @ Q 128 128 2(DB) 128 576 $d{y}$ @ P 128 128 2(DB) 128 512 $Q{index}$ is loaded into L1 at the granularity of basic blocks of $128\times 256$, and permanently resides in L1 during the computation flow of a single basic block, so that it can be reused in the $d{s}$ @ $Q{index}$ computation, reducing repeated memory access. The same technique is also applied to $V{index}$. As shown in the table, in other matrix multiplication computations, limited by L1 space, the source data transfer enables DoubleBuffer to achieve parallelism between transfer and computation. At the same time, the basic block on the UB uses $128\times 128$. SFAG Pipeline Design The computation flow of SparseFlashAttentionScoreGrad includes five stages: the data transfer of $K{index}$ and $V{index}$ from dispersed to contiguous (V0), $Q{index}$@$K{index}$ and $d{y}$@V (C1), computing P and $d{s}$ (V1), computing $d{s}$@K, and finally the dispersed write-out of $d{k}$ and $d{V}$ outside the core (V2). The basic pipeline arrangement strictly following the computation graph is shown in the upper part of the following figure, where multiple stages execute serially, causing a large number of bubbles in the computation process. Here, the optimization is to launch V0 and C1 twice consecutively at the startup stage to resolve the data dependencies of subsequent computations, thereby achieving pipeline masking. The effect is shown in the lower part of the following figure, where the parallel execution between CV greatly reduces the CV data dependency loss. Dispersed Memory-Access Optimization Compared with the traditional FAG, SFAG adds a large number of dispersed memory accesses, and the amount of data in a single access is small, which causes the overhead of the memory-access instructions themselves to be large and prevents the bandwidth from being fully utilized. To address such problems, the Vector cores can be used to rearrange the dispersed data from non-contiguous to contiguous, placing it into a temporary workspace space in basic blocks of $128\times headDim$. When the Cube side launches computation, it can then transfer the input data contiguously, significantly improving bandwidth utilization, as shown in the following figure. FSDP2 + Torch.compile + Inductor Acceleration FSDP2 Prefetch Masking on the A3 Super Node In this practice, as the model parameter count and sequence length surge, communication overhead often becomes the bottleneck restricting cluster scaling efficiency. In the native adaptation of TorchTitan + CANN, we deeply leverage the core feature of FSDP2 — Weight Prefetching — and combine it with the high-bandwidth advantage of the A3 super node to achieve extreme concurrency between computation and communication. 1) FSDP2 weight prefetching: a deterministic communication pipeline FSDP2 is built on DTensor and provides finer-grained communication control capabilities than traditional FSDP. We implemented precise inter-layer pipeline scheduling on the NPU: When the Compute Stream executes the forward or backward computation of the N-th Transformer Block layer, the Communication Stream has already initiated the AllGather operation for the N+1-th layer through asynchronous scheduling, aggregating in advance the full parameters needed by the next layer; at the same time, after the N-th layer computation completes, its parameters are immediately reshared back to each card, releasing memory. This design brings benefits in two aspects: first, it significantly reduces the peak memory usage of model parameters; second, through "prefetching", the compute units do not need to wait for parameters to be in place, achieving true concurrency between communication and computation (Compute-Communication Overlap). However, it should be noted that the premise of communication-computation masking is that the communication time is shorter than the computation time. Prefetch scheduling at the software level alone is not sufficient — if the communication latency is much greater than the computation time, the pipeline will still block. In this regard, the high-bandwidth interconnect architecture of the A3 super node plays a key role. Its high-throughput, low-latency communication capability effectively compresses the time of AllGather, providing the hardware foundation for communication-computation masking. 2) Full communication-computation masking through software-hardware co-design In the actual Profiling of the above figure, it can be observed that the Allgather communication of weight prefetching is almost completely covered by the computation on the Device side. The training pipeline of DeepSeek-V3.2 shows extremely high compactness, and the performance is effectively improved. This result stems from the coordinated cooperation between the FSDP2 prefetch mechanism and the A3 high-bandwidth capability: Software side: FSDP2 precisely schedules communication tasks into the gaps between computations through asynchronous prefetching; Hardware side: The large-bandwidth interconnect of A3 ensures that communication tasks can complete within the computation window, fully hiding the communication latency within the Device-side computation of the NPU. Inductor Graph Optimization Acceleration Even without relying on operator fusion and CUDA Graphs, Inductor still alleviates the Host-bound problem to some extent through Codegen Wrapper and static analysis. It transforms the dynamic scheduling process originally driven line by line by the Python interpreter into a precompiled, efficient computation graph execution flow. By completing operator selection, shape inference, and memory planning at compile time, enabling Inductor compilation can successfully bypass the expensive Dispatcher dispatch mechanism and Python interaction overhead of the PyTorch runtime, speeding up operator dispatch on the host side. Inductor compilation resolves the fixed overhead of dispatching each operator in the original Eager mode during the compilation period, leaving only the most streamlined Kernel Launch scheduling on the host side at runtime. Through Profiling, we can see that the original linear layer contains two operators, aten::t and aten::matmul, which need to go through PythonDispatchMode to dispatch the specific operators, with a total host-side dispatch time of 409.5us; after enabling compile, operator dispatch is completed directly through an executable Python file, and the same four operations take only 118.8us of dispatch time. After enabling inductor: Bypass Automatic Fusion In the Inductor compilation flow, in addition to graph optimization through fxpasses, the following key steps are also included: decompositions decompose complex operators into combinations of basic operators; the lowerings dictionary maps FX nodes to corresponding IR nodes; the Scheduler performs topological sorting and scheduling decisions for operators based on fusion benefits; the Scheduler outputs the fused IR nodes and the corresponding execution plan; finally, the Codegen stage further converts this information into executable Triton Python code. In experiments, we found that the Triton operators generated by Inductor automatic fusion on the current NPU perform poorly in both compilation time and execution performance. Therefore, at this stage, we temporarily bypass the Triton Codegen part of the Inductor flow, and will later integrate Ascend C Codegen to better support complete compilation using the Inductor backend on the NPU. By clearing lowerings and decompositions before compile, most Aten operators will not be decomposed or lowered to the Inductor IR, and will fall back to the original operator implementations. In addition, since GraphLowering adds a requirecontiguous constraint for backward operators without an explicitly specified memory layout, inserting copy (clone) operations for non-contiguous tensors to make them contiguous memory, this operation would convert Aten operators into separate triton operator implementations in the backward stage. We modified the above code to remove the layout operations for backward operators, so that all operators use their original layouts, completely shielding the triton operators. Benchmark Precision Our practice of pretraining the DeepSeek-V3.2 model on the A3 cluster shows that the language model loss (lm loss) and gradient norm (grad norm) converge steadily, demonstrating the stability and efficiency of the TorchTitan framework combined with the TorchTitan-npu adaptation in large-scale model training. The lm loss steadily decreases from 12.25 at step 1 of the initial training to 8.37 at step 37, maintaining a continuously decreasing trend throughout with no obvious oscillation; the gradient synchronously falls smoothly from the initial 28.24 to 16.03, generally trending toward convergence with no abnormal fluctuations. At the same time, the Lighting Indexer proposed for the DeepSeek-V3.2 network was also trained. Throughout the pretraining process, the indexer loss decreases steadily and maintains a smooth downward trend. Combined with the lm loss and grad norm curves, this proves that the precision is normal in large-scale distributed scenarios and can efficiently support the pretraining task of the DeepSeek-V3.2 model. Performance Currently, through the optimization of fused operators and inductor, TorchTitan-npu can achieve fairly obvious performance improvements on the basis of the implementation using Torch native small operators; in the future, when the Inductor backend integrates the Ascend-native Ascend C Codegen, even more obvious performance gains are expected. Fused Operators Through the lightweight plug-in approach mentioned earlier, support for NPU basic fused operators can be achieved without modifying the torchtitan code. Currently, four basic fused operators — RMSNorm, Rope, GMM, and permute/unpermute — and the DeepSeek-V3.2 model DSA fused operators (LI/SFA/LIG) are supported, and they can be enabled simply by configuring converters in the training configuration toml file. Since the original small-operator implementation has large memory overhead, we compared the performance with the small-operator implementation on an 8-layer trimmed model (1 dense layer, 7 moe layers, each moe layer with 8 experts) and a 4-layer trimmed model (1 dense layer, 3 moe layers, each moe layer with 8 experts), with a training length of 4k. The performance and memory conditions are as follows: Trimmed model Implementation Memory Performance -------------------------------------------------------------- 8-layer trimmed model Original small-operator implementation 58.32G 155TPS 8-layer trimmed model Matrix absorption + DSA fused operators 50.54G 400TPS 4-layer trimmed model Original small-operator implementation 54.58G 402TPS 4-layer trimmed model Matrix absorption + DSA fused operators 38.71G 568TPS After enabling the DSA fused operators, the DeepSeek-V3.2 model can not only significantly reduce memory usage during training, but also improve computation speed. Further enabling the basic fused operators, the computation time within a single step is reduced by 5.16% on the complete DeepSeek-V3.2 model. The experiment collected the device-side execution times before and after enabling the fused operators: Operator type Time before fusion Time after fusion Time saved Performance improvement ratio ----------------------------------------------------- RMSNorm 138.7μs 39.9μs 98.8μs 71.2% Permute 803.9μs 127.3μs 676.6μs 84.2% GMM 3.1ms 2.4ms 0.7ms 22.6% torch.compile We referenced the applycompile approach in the original TorchTitan code, which performs whole-graph compilation for each transformer block, and split the complete Attention part into three parts: MLAProlog, innerattention, and MLAEpilog. Since innerattention is already implemented with DSA fused operators, the host side does not need to dispatch too many small operators, so whether to compile has little impact on the overall performance. We compile the MLAProlog and MLAEpilog parts as well as the router, gate, etc. in the MoE part, alleviating the host-side dispatch overhead caused by the large number of small operators. After enabling compile, the MLAProlog case with obvious host bound is significantly optimized. The original host-side dispatch times: Host-side dispatch time Device-side compute execution time --------- Before enabling compile 11.0ms 10.7ms After enabling compile 5.7ms 4.5ms Measured on the complete DeepSeek-V3.2 model, after enabling inductor compile, the per-layer time is reduced by 5.1%. Since the computation time of the DeepSeek-V3.2 model is concentrated in the main operators such as SFA and LI, enabling inductor for host-side dispatch optimization has limited effect on improving the overall network performance. Future Plan TorchTitan-npu currently mainly focuses on compatibility with the community ecosystem, migrating the simple and easy-to-use native PyTorch TorchTitan ecosystem to NPUs, so that the community can quickly migrate training tasks to Ascend chips for deployment, enriching the CANN training ecosystem; in the future, we will continue to optimize the out-of-the-box performance based on torch.compile; the current SFAG operator will be upgraded in the next CANN version to greatly improve performance; in addition, we will continue to evolve in the following directions: Ascend C Autofuse Integration The Inductor component of the PyTorch framework in graph mode provides the basic operator fusion and compilation capabilities for this purpose, and its design is compatible with the existing PyTorch ecosystem, with good software inheritance. However, since there are essential differences between NPU and GPU in memory architecture, compute units, and parallel mechanisms, directly adopting GPU-oriented optimization strategies cannot fully unleash the hardware potential of the NPU. Therefore, at this stage, the Bypass Triton approach is used to circumvent the performance insufficiency of the Triton backend on the NPU. To achieve efficient fusion for the NPU while inheriting the overall Inductor flow and interfaces, it is necessary to have NPU-oriented Just-In-Time (JIT) operator generation capability. To this end, the AutoFuse component inherited by the CANN framework has been deeply optimized for the architectural characteristics of the NPU, achieving automated mapping and generation from computation graphs to efficient NPU operator code. This component not only maintains synergy and compatibility with Inductor technology, but also further significantly improves the execution efficiency of operator fusion on the NPU through architecture-aware fusion strategies, memory-access optimization, and instruction scheduling, thereby supporting high-performance deployment of complex models on NPU platforms. As a result, it will further improve the performance of the inductor-compiled model. DualPipeV Support DualPipeV is an efficient Pipeline Parallelism (PP) scheduling strategy specifically designed for large-scale MoE models (such as DeepSeek-V3). It originates from DualPipe designed by the DeepSeek team and draws on InterLeave1F1B . The core design concept of DualPipeV is: a single device can simultaneously host one forward computation batch and one backward computation batch, and the communication and computation of the two can run in parallel with each other. In this way, the computation of one batch can largely mask the communication overhead brought by MoE EP parallelism. The TorchTitan community has preliminarily supported the DualPipeV feature, but in practice it was found that DualPipeV cannot be enabled in the ZeRO3 DP partitioning scenario. The reason is that the native torch dW computation implementation constrains the weight W from maintaining the partitioned state in the DP domain. To obtain both memory and performance benefits, TorchTitan will be adapted later to enable ZeRO3 and DualPipeV simultaneously. TPasync Support TP completes cross-card synchronization within a layer through AllGather and ReduceScatter, and the communication latency is directly exposed on the critical path. The core idea of Async TP is to decompose the communication and computation operators simultaneously — AllGather is split into multiple Send/Recv operations, and Matmul is split into corresponding sub-Matmuls — so that the computation of one sub-Matmul executes concurrently with the data transfer of the next chunk, thereby hiding the communication latency. In TorchTitan-npu, at the FX computation graph stage, the Inductor compiler can recognize patterns such as allgather + matmul or matmul + reduce-scatter, and automatically complete this decomposition and reordering without modifying the model code. Combined with the high-bandwidth inter-card interconnect within the A3 node, intra-layer TP communication can be effectively compressed and hidden within the computation window.

DeepSeek-V4昇腾训练支持：基于 CANN 平台的TorchTitan-NPU + AutoFuse 极简训练优化实践 摘要：本文介绍 DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash 模型基于 CANN 平台的训练优化实践。基于 TorchTitan\-NPU 框架，采用纯 FSDP + 大 EP 极简并行策略实现内存最优；创新性地使能训练入图技术，凭借 Ascend C AutoFuse 能力，获得端到端 32% 的编译收益；针对稀疏注意力结构定制高效融合算子，充分释放芯片算力。DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash 模型在 64 卡 A3 集群上 4K 序列 BF16 训练吞吐达 1100 tokens/p/s。这一快速支持能力验证了极简开箱方案在 NPU 大模型训练中的可行性与高效性，旨在帮助现有昇腾 A3 集群用户基于 DeepSeek 新模型架构快速开展续训练/SFT 及自研算法验证。 本文涉及的所有代码已开源： torchtitan-npu 开源仓库 ，快速体验见 《基于TorchTitan-NPU的DeepSeek-V4-Flash训练部署指导》 。 Highlights 训练框架采用 TorchTitan + TorchTitan\-NPU 插件化方案，采用超节点亲和的大 EP + 纯 FSDP 的精简并行切分策略，以极低适配成本和通信开销达成内存占用最优，实现易用性与性能的较好均衡 TorchTitan\-NPU 深度适配 torch.compile 机制，使能训练入图技术，依托 Inductor + AutoFuse（基于 Ascend C 的 Codegen 后端）实现端到端的 Vector 算子自动融合，为整网带来高达 31.8% 的开箱即用性能收益 针对稀疏注意力等复杂结构，开发 SparseAttnSharedkv、LightningIndexer 等多个高效的 NPU 融合算子，从负载均衡分核计算、内存与计算均衡等维度协同优化，充分释放芯片稀疏算力 基于上述优化点，CANN 已基于 TorchTitan 支持 DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash 的模型训练，采用 A3 集群 BF16 精度 64 卡 4K 序列 + MTP1 训练吞吐达 1100 tokens/p/s 引言 TorchTitan 为业界带来了 PyTorch Native 大模型训练方案的全新选择，其核心设计理念是模型算法与分布式并行、算子优化天然解耦。通过支持 torch.compile 训练入图优化，告别手写融合 kernel，大大提升了大规模分布式训练的易用性。在并行策略方面，TorchTitan 深度集成 FSDP2，实现参数、梯度和优化器状态的跨设备分片，显著降低单卡内存占用。 本实践的整体软件架构自顶向下由 TorchTitan、TorchTitan\-NPU 插件、TorchInductor 及 CANN 层的 AutoFuse 组件构成，各层分工明确、优势互补： TorchTitan：作为 PyTorch 原生分布式训练框架，避免对 Megatron 等重型框架的依赖，以精简代码库提供 FSDP 等并行能力的开箱即用支持。 TorchTitan\-NPU：以插件形式提供可插拔安装，针对昇腾集群实现通信与算子的硬件加速适配，保持与上游 TorchTitan 的轻量集成。 TorchInductor：直接继承社区 torch.compile 的图捕获与融合优化能力，无需重复造轮即可复用 PyTorch 编译生态的相关基础设施。 AutoFuse：面向昇腾 NPU，定位为基于 Ascend C 的 Codegen & Schedule 后端，在 Inductor 基础上注入架构感知的融合、优化与展开策略，将计算图优化转化为 NPU 高效指令序列。 Architecture 基于上述分层架构，我们在 TorchTitan\-NPU 加速插件的基础上完成了 DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash 模型续训练流程的适配与调优。整个方案围绕“极简并行、自动融合、定制算子”三条主线展开，下文将分别就基于 FSDP+EP 的极简分布式并行、torch.compile 与 AutoFuse 自动融合协同、以及高性能融合算子优化加速进行详细阐述。 极简分布式并行优化 FSDP+EP极简切分优势 在 MoE 大模型训练中，EP 切分可有效分摊路由专家权重的存储压力，但注意力模块、共享专家、词嵌入及词表投影层等非专家参数仍需额外切分机制加以应对。另一方面，随着模型结构迎来又一个快速发展阶段，传统 TP/PP 方案在性能开销与易用性层面均面临诸多挑战，而 FSDP 在上述场景中展现出较为显著的优势。因此，本实践基于 A3 超节点 64 卡环境，在 DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash 模型训练中创新性地选择纯 FSDP + EP 极简切分方案，具体配置如下： TPPPVPPEPFSDPMBSGBS集群 ------------------------ 1111281281102464卡 FSDP简介 FSDP（Fully Sharded Data Parallel）是 PyTorch 提供的数据并行技术，通过将模型参数、梯度和优化器状态跨设备分片存储，显著降低单卡内存占用。其原理是将 DDP 的 AllReduce 分解为前向的 AllGather 与后向的 ReduceScatter，在计算过程中按需收集参数、用完即释，以最小化常驻内存。此外，FSDP 的通信操作可与计算重叠执行，AllGather 提前预取下一层参数，ReduceScatter 则在后向计算进行时同步传输，有效将通信延迟掩盖在计算耗时内。 FSDP-Illustration 内存收益 尽管 MoE 模型的路由专家权重在全局参数量中占据绝对主导，但经过 EP 维度切分后，非路由专家权重在单卡内存中的占比将显著上升，成为新的内存瓶颈。下表以 DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash 模型为例展示了 EP 切分前后瓶颈的转换，其中主权重和模型梯度均按照混合精度训练场景下常见的 4 字节大小计算。 FSDP DP EP 总参数量 非专家参数量 非专家权重+梯度 专家参数量 专家权重+梯度 非专家内存占比 1 128 1 285B 8B 59.5GB 277B 2060GB 2.8% 1 128 128 285B 8B 59.5GB 2B 16GB 80% 128 1 128 285B 0.06B 0.465GB 2B 16GB 2.8% 考虑到 A3 单卡 64GB 的内存大小，在模型训练过程中不可避免地需要引入对非专家参数的切分。对比 TP/PP，FSDP 的通信可被计算完全掩盖（详见性能小节），因而可以使用相对激进的内存切分配置而不受性能考量的制约。实测开启 FSDP128 后，非专家权重被均分至全部 128 DIE，几乎完全消除该部分内存占用——TorchTitan 完成模型初始化后单卡权重内存仅约 89GB，可视作仅由 EP 切分后的路由专家权重构成。 FSDP-vs-TP-PP 性能开销 FSDP 通信数据不依赖当前层的中间计算结果，框架得以将集合通信操作下发至独立的通信流上，与模型前向/反向计算异步并发执行。借助于 A3 超节点的高通信带宽，实测 FSDP 的通信开销可被计算过程完全掩盖。这一特性打破了性能与内存之间的折衷——采用 FSDP128 将通信域扩大到 8 机范围时，依然不会因通信暴露而损害训练吞吐，为内存侧的极致压缩提供了可行性保障。 FSDP-overlapped 与之相对地，TP/PP 中的通信与计算关键路径紧密耦合，无法掩盖。即使借助 A3 芯片的 SIO 高带宽通信，并采用 TP2 这类极小通信域配置，张量并行依然会带来可观的通信开销；另一方面，PP 切分的流水线气泡率随通信域规模的扩大同步增加，导致的设备空闲亦不可忽略。这些现实约束反过来制约了数据并行向 TP/PP 的转换，实际部署中往往无法将数据并行完全切分为 TP/PP，从而残留一定程度的内存冗余。 易用性优势 除内存与性能优势外，FSDP 在工程复杂度上也显著优于 TP/PP： 对 TP 切分而言，DeepSeek 系列模型中 MLA/DSA/C4A/C128A 结构的引入使得注意力机制的 TP 切分越来越复杂。DeepSeek\-V4 的注意力机制在整体框架上继承了 DeepSeek\-V3.2 引入的 DSA 结构，其 Indexer 模块在计算前向结果和 Loss 值时均涉及模型 head 维度的累加操作，如下图所示。该操作的语义决定了无法直接沿 head 维度进行 TP 切分——强行切分则需同时引入新的 AllGather 聚合通信，以保证 ReduceSum 的正确性。 Indexer-TP 对 PP 切分而言，模型中非均匀的模块（Embedding、LmHead、MTP 等）极易导致 PP Stage 间的耗时不均，MoE 模型中本身与数据分布相关的负载不均衡现象更进一步加重了 PP 性能调优过程中的困难。 相较之下，FSDP 对参数无差异分片并作异步 AllGather 的方式做到了模型算法和结构无感的权重切分——前反向计算时总可以获取完整的单层模型权重，各个 DP rank 间执行的计算无任何差异，且在适配上仅通过一行 fullyshard 函数调用即可，较好地克服了前述场景中 TP/PP 的缺陷。 双通信域overlap优化 基于 FSDP 相对于 TP/PP 的上述优势，我们选择了 FSDP128 + EP128 作为模型的切分策略，并在实际测试中优化了 TorchTitan 上游实现存在的一个通信域初始化问题：由于前述切分策略中，FSDP 域和 EP 域均与分布式并行组的全局默认通信域相同，使得 PyTorch 为 FSDP 和 EP 分配同一个 ProcessGroup，导致两者的通信操作被迫串行执行，无法并发。 FSDP-EP-bug 具体而言，如上图所示，EP 通信位于 MoE 模型执行的关键路径上，任何阻塞都会直接延迟模型的整体计算。当 FSDP 与 EP 共享 ProcessGroup 时，FSDP 的 AllGather/ReduceScatter 会与 EP 的 AllToAll 形成串行等待关系：FSDP 的通信操作会阻塞 EP 通信的执行，并最终进一步阻塞后续的计算算子。这意味着原本设计中被计算隐藏的 FSDP 通信暴露到了关键路径上，造成整体吞吐下降。 FSDP-EP-bugfix 通过在初始化阶段对 EP 通信域进行独立标注，FSDP 与 EP 得以持有各自的 ProcessGroup。两者的通信操作因此可在不同的 HCCL 流上并发执行，从而恢复 FSDP 通信被模型主计算流程掩盖的设计初衷。修复后，EP DeepSeek-V4 Ascend Training Support: Minimalist Training Optimization Practice of TorchTitan-NPU + AutoFuse on the CANN Platform Abstract: This article introduces the training optimization practice of the DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash model based on the CANN platform. Built on the TorchTitan\-NPU framework, it adopts the pure FSDP + large EP minimalist parallel strategy to achieve optimal memory usage; innovatively enables the training-graph technology and, leveraging the Ascend C AutoFuse capability, obtains an end-to-end 32% compilation benefit; for the sparse attention structure, it customizes high-efficiency fused operators to fully unleash chip compute power. The DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash model achieves a training throughput of 1100 tokens/p/s on a 64-card A3 cluster with 4K-sequence BF16 training. This rapid support capability validates the feasibility and efficiency of the minimalist out-of-the-box solution in NPU large-model training, aiming to help existing Ascend A3 cluster users quickly carry out continued training/SFT and self-developed algorithm validation based on the new DeepSeek model architecture. All code involved in this article is open source: torchtitan-npu repository . For a quick hands-on experience, see DeepSeek-V4-Flash Training Deployment Guide Based on TorchTitan-NPU (Chinese). Highlights The training framework adopts the TorchTitan + TorchTitan\-NPU plugin-based solution, using a streamlined parallel partitioning strategy of super-node-affinity large EP + pure FSDP to achieve optimal memory usage with extremely low adaptation cost and communication overhead, striking a good balance between usability and performance TorchTitan\-NPU deeply adapts to the torch.compile mechanism and enables the training-graph technology. Relying on Inductor + AutoFuse (an Ascend C-based Codegen backend), it implements end-to-end automatic fusion of Vector operators, delivering up to 31.8% out-of-the-box performance gains for the entire network For complex structures such as sparse attention, we developed multiple high-efficiency NPU fused operators including SparseAttnSharedkv and LightningIndexer, collaboratively optimizing from dimensions such as load-balanced split-core computation and memory-computation balance, fully unleashing the chip's sparse compute power Based on the above optimizations, CANN already supports DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash model training based on TorchTitan, achieving a training throughput of 1100 tokens/p/s on an A3 cluster with BF16 precision, 64 cards, 4K sequence + MTP1 Introduction TorchTitan brings the industry a brand-new option for PyTorch Native large-model training solutions. Its core design philosophy is to naturally decouple model algorithms from distributed parallelism and operator optimization. By supporting torch.compile training-graph optimization, it eliminates hand-written fused kernels and greatly improves the usability of large-scale distributed training. In terms of parallel strategies, TorchTitan deeply integrates FSDP2, achieving cross-device sharding of parameters, gradients, and optimizer states, significantly reducing per-card memory usage. The overall software architecture of this practice, from top to bottom, consists of TorchTitan, the TorchTitan\-NPU plugin, TorchInductor, and the AutoFuse component at the CANN layer. Each layer has clear responsibilities and complementary strengths: TorchTitan: As a PyTorch-native distributed training framework, it avoids dependence on heavyweight frameworks such as Megatron, providing out-of-the-box support for parallel capabilities like FSDP with a streamlined codebase. TorchTitan\-NPU: Provided as a pluggable, installable plugin, it implements hardware-accelerated adaptation of communication and operators for Ascend clusters while maintaining lightweight integration with upstream TorchTitan. TorchInductor: It directly inherits the graph capture and fusion optimization capabilities of the community torch.compile, reusing the relevant infrastructure of the PyTorch compilation ecosystem without reinventing the wheel. AutoFuse: Targeted at Ascend NPUs, it is positioned as an Ascend C-based Codegen & Schedule backend. On top of Inductor, it injects architecture-aware fusion, optimization, and expansion strategies to transform computation graph optimization into efficient NPU instruction sequences. Architecture Based on the above layered architecture, we completed the adaptation and tuning of the DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash model continued-training workflow on top of the TorchTitan\-NPU acceleration plugin. The entire solution revolves around three main threads: "minimalist parallelism, automatic fusion, and custom operators". The following sections elaborate on the minimalist distributed parallelism based on FSDP+EP, the collaboration between torch.compile and AutoFuse automatic fusion, and high-performance fused operator optimization and acceleration. Minimalist Distributed Parallelism Optimization Advantages of the Minimalist FSDP+EP Partitioning In MoE large-model training, EP partitioning can effectively share the storage pressure of routed expert weights, but non-expert parameters such as the attention module, shared experts, word embeddings, and vocabulary projection layers still require additional partitioning mechanisms. On the other hand, as model architectures enter another phase of rapid development, traditional TP/PP schemes face numerous challenges in both performance overhead and usability, while FSDP demonstrates relatively significant advantages in the above scenarios. Therefore, based on the A3 super-node 64-card environment, this practice innovatively chooses the pure FSDP + EP minimalist partitioning scheme in DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash model training, with the specific configuration as follows: TPPPVPPEPFSDPMBSGBSCluster ------------------------ 1111281281102464 cards Introduction to FSDP FSDP (Fully Sharded Data Parallel) is a data parallelism technique provided by PyTorch. It significantly reduces per-card memory usage by sharding model parameters, gradients, and optimizer states across devices. Its principle is to decompose DDP's AllReduce into a forward AllGather and a backward ReduceScatter, collecting parameters on demand during computation and releasing them immediately after use to minimize resident memory. In addition, FSDP's communication operations can overlap with computation: AllGather prefetches the next layer's parameters in advance, while ReduceScatter transfers synchronously during backward computation, effectively hiding communication latency within computation time. FSDP-Illustration Memory Benefits Although routed expert weights in MoE models absolutely dominate the global parameter count, after EP-dimensional partitioning, the proportion of non-routed expert weights in per-card memory rises significantly and becomes a new memory bottleneck. The following table uses the DeepSeek\-V4\-Flash model as an example to show the bottleneck shift before and after EP partitioning, where master weights and model gradients are both calculated based on the common 4-byte size in mixed-precision training scenarios. Compared with TP/PP, FSDP's communication can be completely hidden by computation (see the performance section for details), so a relatively aggressive memory partitioning configuration can be used without being constrained by performance considerations. In measurements, after enabling FSDP128, non-expert weights are evenly distributed across all 128 DIE, almost completely eliminating this portion of memory usage — after TorchTitan completes model initialization, the per-card weight memory is only about 89GB, which can be considered to consist solely of routed expert weights after EP partitioning. FSDP-vs-TP-PP Performance Overhead FSDP communication data does not depend on the intermediate computation results of the current layer, so the framework can dispatch collective communication operations to an independent communication stream to execute asynchronously and concurrently with the model's forward/backward computation. Thanks to the high communication bandwidth of the A3 super-node, measured FSDP communication overhead can be completely hidden by the computation process. This property breaks the trade-off between performance and memory — when FSDP128 expands the communication domain to 8 machines, training throughput is still not degraded by exposed communication, providing feasibility guarantees for extreme compression on the memory side. FSDP-overlapped In contrast, communication in TP/PP is tightly coupled with the critical path of computation and cannot be hidden. Even with the SIO high-bandwidth communication of the A3 chip and extremely small communication domain configurations such as TP2, tensor parallelism still introduces considerable communication overhead. On the other hand, the pipeline bubble rate of PP partitioning increases synchronously with the expansion of the communication domain scale, and the resulting device idle time is also non-negligible. These practical constraints in turn restrict the conversion of data parallelism into TP/PP, and in actual deployments data parallelism often cannot be fully partitioned into TP/PP, leaving a certain degree of memory redundancy. Usability Advantages In addition to memory and performance advantages, FSDP is also significantly better than TP/PP in engineering complexity: For TP partitioning, the introduction of MLA/DSA/C4A/C128A structures in the DeepSeek series models makes TP partitioning of the attention mechanism increasingly complex. The attention mechanism of DeepSeek\-V4 inherits, in its overall framework, the DSA structure introduced by DeepSeek\-V3.2. Its Indexer module involves accumulation operations along the model head dimension when computing both forward results and Loss values, as shown in the figure below. The semantics of this operation determine that TP partitioning cannot be performed directly along the head dimension — forcing such partitioning would require simultaneously introducing new AllGather aggregation communication to ensure the correctness of ReduceSum. Indexer-TP For PP partitioning, non-uniform modules in the model (Embedding, LmHead, MTP, etc.) can easily lead to uneven time consumption across PP stages, and the load imbalance inherent to data distribution in MoE models further aggravates the difficulty of PP performance tuning. In contrast, FSDP's approach of indiscriminately sharding parameters with asynchronous AllGather achieves weight partitioning that is agnostic to model algorithms and structures — during forward/backward computation, the complete single-layer model weights can always be obtained, and the computation executed across DP ranks has no differences. Moreover, adaptation requires only a single-line fullyshard function call, which effectively overcomes the shortcomings of TP/PP in the aforementioned scenarios. Dual Communication Domain Overlap Optimization Based on the above advantages of FSDP over TP/PP, we selected FSDP128 + EP128 as the model partitioning strategy, and during actual testing optimized a communication domain initialization problem in the upstream TorchTitan implementation: in the aforementioned partitioning strategy, both the FSDP domain and the EP domain are identical to the global default communication domain of the distributed parallel group, causing PyTorch to assign the same ProcessGroup to FSDP and EP, which forces their communication operations to execute serially and prevents concurrency. FSDP-EP-bug Specifically, as shown in the figure above, EP communication lies on the critical path of MoE model execution, and any blocking directly delays the overall computation of the model. When FSDP and EP share a ProcessGroup, FSDP's AllGather/ReduceScatter forms a serial waiting relationship with EP's AllToAll: FSDP's communication operations block the execution of EP communication, and ultimately further block subsequent computation operators. This means that the FSDP communication originally designed to be hidden by computation is exposed to the critical path, causing overall throughput degradation. FSDP-EP-bugfix By independently marking the EP communication domain during the initialization phase, FSDP and EP are able to hold their own ProcessGroups. Their communication operations can therefore execute concurrently on different HCCL streams, restoring the design intent that FSDP communication be hidden by the model's main computation flow. After the fix, the critical-path communication of EP is no longer blocked by FSDP. Measured results show that the fix reduces the communication wait time of the model at the MoE layer from a maximum of 10ms to 3ms, bringing a 1.1% improvement in model training performance. We will later feed this issue back to the PyTorch/TorchTitan upstream community, hoping to facilitate optimization of the framework in subsequent versions. Memory Offload Optimization In the native FSDP2 solution, although parameters, gradients, and optimizer states are all partitioned, AdamW's two FP32 momenta still reside in device memory during forward/backward computation, resulting in idle waste. As a memory optimization supplement to FSDP, SwapOptimizer (Chinese) further offloads the optimizer states that FSDP has partitioned to a single card to host memory, swapping them in on demand only during the weight update phase. We implemented this feature in TorchTitan by referencing the MindSpeed approach, adapting it to the DTensor weight scenario, and designing a slice pipeline at parameter granularity to overlap the serial "load-update-offload" process in the manner shown in the figure below, reducing the memory peak during the optimizer update phase. Swap-optimizer This mechanism further reduces the resident memory in the AdamW optimizer scenario from FSDP's 16 bytes/parameter (weight 4 + gradient 4 + optimizer 8) to 8 bytes/parameter (weight + gradient only), nearly halving memory usage. torch.compile + AutoFuse With the proliferation of MoE and multimodal architectures, dynamic, fine-grained compositions of small operators have become the mainstream design pattern. Taking the mHC proposed by DeepSeek as an example, it decomposes the HC process into three parts — HcRes, HcPre, and HcPost — which guarantee mathematical properties through doubly stochastic matrices and Sigmoid gating coefficients respectively, but the implementation relies on a large number of fragmented PyTorch operations. Such flexible structures are increasingly common in model design. If the traditional approach of hand-writing fused operators is continued, development efficiency can no longer keep pace with model iteration speed, making automatic operator fusion capability a rigid requirement. mHC torch.compile provides the foundational capability for this: by capturing the FX computation graph, it converts model logic into an operator graph representation, which is handed to the Inductor backend for operator fusion and code generation. Through vertical and horizontal fusion strategies, Inductor merges multiple fragmented operations into a single efficient kernel, achieving cross-operator global optimization. TorchTitan provides native deep support for torch.compile, fully reusing PyTorch's existing compilation ecosystem infrastructure and optimization results. However, NPUs and GPUs differ fundamentally in memory architecture and computational paradigm, and directly applying GPU optimization strategies cannot fully unleash NPU potential. To this end, the AutoFuse component of the CANN framework, based on inheriting the overall Inductor flow, implements a Schedule & Codegen backend targeting Ascend C. Through architecture-aware fusion strategies and instruction scheduling, it achieves automatic mapping from computation graphs to efficient NPU operator code, significantly improving the execution efficiency of fused operators on Ascend platforms. AutoFuse In the training scenario of this practice, since TP partitioning is not enabled, the computation volume of each operator is inherently large, and after operator fusion the Kernel Launch overhead accounts for an extremely low proportion, leaving no room for static-graph benefits. Therefore, we adopt the dynamic-graph Eager mode to execute the compiled operator graph. Moreover, the Eager mode does not need to handle dynamic Shape constraints, making it simpler and more flexible while still capturing the main performance benefits of fusion. 基于verl前端&A3集群的DeepSeek-R1模型RL训练优化实践 1. 前言 1.1 背景 DeepSeek-R1发布后，大模型的RL训练得到了广泛的关注，各大厂商以及开源社区都进行了大量的RL训练实践，致力于构建更高效的RL训练系统。本文基于开源的verl框架，搭配MindSpeed与vLLM Ascend框架，经过深入优化与适配，在Atlas A3 SuperPoD超节点上实现了高吞吐性能。 本文中涉及的开源框架如下表所示。 框架名称 介绍 ----- ---- verl 开源LLM强化学习框架，结合单控制器（控制流）与多控制器（计算流）优势，简化了RL算法（如PPO、GRPO）实现。其训练支持FSDP、FSDP2与Megatron-LM，推理支持vLLM、SGLang与HFTransformers。 vLLM 为大语言模型提供高吞吐量和内存高效推理服务的开源引擎，使用PagedAttention技术高效实现KVcache的内存管理，并支持众推理特性。 vLLM Ascend vLLM的昇腾NPU适配插件，支持NPU上的诸多优化。本实践过程中的一些优化贡献到了该开源仓。 Megatron-LM 超大规模语言模型训练框架，支持多种分布式并行策略。 MindSpeed 针对NPU的大模型训练加速库，提供Megatron-LM框架对NPU的基本功能适配以及一些亲和NPU的优化特性。 MindSpeed RL 基于昇腾生态的强化学习加速框架，本优化实践对其进行了一些借鉴参考。 1.2 技术路径选择 1.2.1 为何选择全共卡部署？ DeepSeek R1的每一步训练可大致分为三个计算密集的阶段：推理生成完整问答数据（rollout/generate）-> 参考模型计算参考概率分布（ref）-> 训练模型计算loss并反向更新（update）；对于DeepSeek R1这个具有671B参数的大模型而言，以上三个阶段都需要大量的计算资源。因此，rollout/ref/update三个模型共卡部署、分时复用计算资源是一种简单高效的部署策略。 此外，rollout部分我们并未采用推理常用的PD分离部署策略（即Prefill阶段与Decode阶段分别实例化部署在不同的机器资源），因为整个RL训练中推理Prefill部分耗时占比很小，优化收益不高。 1.2.2 为何选择vLLM Ascend？ vLLM Ascend通过硬件插件化机制解耦了框架与硬件依赖，用户无需修改核心代码即可在昇腾NPU上部署模型，代码完全开源，且持续进行新特性适配。目前vLLM Ascend已经支持vLLM的V1模式，并针对DeepSeek-R1的TorchAir图模式进行了优化，这对于rollout部分的优化很有必要。 1.3 verl适配和优化实践总览 ------------------------- ray给一个worker下发任务都包括至少三步：输入数据序列化、数据传输、输出数据序列化。因此，当任务的输入tensor数据量很大时，大量worker的任务下发耗时会不断累积，从而造成训练性能瓶颈。 此外，相较于训练侧任务，generate\sequences任务下发耗时在一秒内，也能从侧面证明任务下发耗时与数据量有关。如下图所示，gen输入数据量远小于训练侧输入数据量，原因是多方面的： 此外，本实践尝试将verl中ray下发任务改为多线程并行，但实测并不能满足需要： ref计算任务下发只能从66秒减少至24秒，难以实现任务下发耗时全部消除的效果。 多线程并行下发任务会导致某些worker存在tensor数据序列化出错，难以解决。 通过梳理优化方案的设计方向，本实践决定主要朝以下两个目标发力。 目标1：减少数据在任务间传递的耗时。 根据此前分析，verl在NPU上大规模训练时性能较差，主要是串行任务下发过程中包含每个worker输入数据的序列化、ray传输、反序列化。但其实大多训练侧任务的输入数据由前序任务产生在device侧，将数据发送至host侧，由主进程调整后再发送回device侧，此流程从性能角度来看并不合理。 可以考虑利用AlltoAllV集合通信直接实现D2D数据直传来加速verl任务间的数据流，即原本的主进程collect+dispatch处理数据的逻辑使用AlltoAllV在device间通信过程中直接实现。此外，由于我们verl训练中actor模型与ref模型并行策略一致，DP rank排布完全一致，所以ref使用过的输入输出数据与update所需输入数据完全一致，甚至可以省掉集合通信操作。 目标2：任务控制维持verl单控制器的逻辑。 verl上层用Ray做调度，在worker间传递数据，实现RL算法的控制流，也就是所谓的单控制器。verl单控制器的优势是架构清晰，简化不同的RL算法在框架下的实现：只需要写好worker的方法，然后在主进程训练流程中择机调用即可。 而数据在多个worker之间直接通信传递属于多控制器逻辑，会将RL训练中任务间控制逻辑的实现复杂化，与verl框架原本的设计理念不符。 可以考虑将verl的控制流与数据流解耦开来，数据流尽可能使用D2D直传加速，控制流逻辑维持不变：采用cache的方式，将后续任务同样会使用的数据在device侧原地缓存，后续任务执行时按需从缓存中拉取；其他必须返回至CPU侧的数据、必须从CPU侧获取的数据维持原本与控制流耦合的逻辑。 3.2.2 总体流程 我们使用TensorCache在device管理前后任务间共用的tensor，从而加速传输速度，减少任务下发耗时。对于单个worker而言，新方案中任务间的流程大致如下： 以下时序图展示了方案的收益来源：主要为数据流加速后，任务下发至worker的耗时大大减少，worker间任务启动时差大大降低。
